title: ART, Zygote, system_server & Build Artifacts
scopeHtml: Scope: how Android processes are born (Zygote), what system_server's services do, how code is packaged (DEX, APK/AAB), how ART runs and compiles it, and the platform-level hazards (hidden APIs, desugaring, R8, ABIs). Profiling and Baseline Profile practice belong to A6; Binder internals to chunk 14.

notes.title: Zygote
notes.html:
What it is. Zygote is the "mother process" of every Android app. Starting a full runtime plus all framework classes takes a long time, so Android does it once at boot, and every new app is a fork (a cheap copy) of that already-warm process.

Mechanism. init starts app_process from init.zygote64.rc (and zygote32 on devices with 32-bit support). Zygote starts ART, preloads about thousands of framework classes and resources (preloaded-classes, boot image boot.art/boot.oat, fonts, shared libraries), then opens a socket (/dev/socket/zygote) and waits. It forks system_server first, then on request forks each app process. fork() is copy-on-write: parent and child share the same physical pages until one writes. That is why every app's "Code" and boot-image memory is mostly shared (low PSS) and why app start is tens of milliseconds for the fork rather than seconds.

init -> zygote (preload classes, boot image)
          |-- fork -> system_server
          |-- fork -> com.example.app   (specialize: set uid, gid, SELinux context, nice name)
          |-- fork -> com.android.chrome

Details. After fork the child "specializes": setuid, SELinux domain, seccomp filter, process name, then loads your APK and calls ActivityThread.main. Zygote itself must stay single-threaded when forking (threads such as the HeapTaskDaemon are stopped and restarted around the fork), and must not hold per-app secrets. Address-space layout randomization is the reason Zygote uses "ASLR is shared": all apps share the same layout of Zygote-loaded libraries (a known security trade-off, hence pre-fork randomization work in newer versions).

Real examples. The fast start of Instagram or WhatsApp from a cold process owes its first few hundred milliseconds to Zygote forking, not to your code. Booting a custom ROM with a broken preloaded-classes shows as extremely slow app starts.

Real-life picture. A restaurant with a pre-prepared base curry: each order starts from the same pot (fork) and only the last spices (your app) differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying each app starts a fresh Dalvik/ART VM from scratch.
  • Forgetting copy-on-write: sharing lasts only until pages are written.
  • Not knowing system_server is also forked from Zygote.

notes.title: system_server services
notes.html:
What it is. system_server is the single most important process: it hosts the Java system services that apps talk to through Binder. If it dies, the Android framework restarts (a "soft reboot").

Key services (all run in system_server).

Service Role
ActivityManagerService (AMS) process lifecycle, services, broadcasts, providers, OOM adj
ActivityTaskManagerService (ATMS, since 10) Activities, tasks, Recents, back stack
WindowManagerService (WMS) windows, focus, input routing, transitions
PackageManagerService (PMS) install, intent resolution, permissions data
PowerManagerService, JobSchedulerService, AlarmManagerService wake locks, jobs, alarms
NotificationManagerService, InputManagerService, ConnectivityService, LocationManagerService as the names say

Some services live elsewhere (SurfaceFlinger, mediaserver/audioserver, cameraserver, servicemanager, netd). Apps never call these classes directly: they get a proxy from Context.getSystemService() that wraps a Binder.

Why it matters. All your startActivity, startService, registerReceiver, permission checks and job scheduling are transactions into system_server. A slow system_server (lock contention, too many Binder calls) makes every app feel sluggish. Binder threads in system_server are limited (default 31 per process), so floods of calls are a real risk.

Real examples. An app that registers hundreds of alarms or broadcast receivers burdens AMS/AlarmManager; Android vitals' "excessive wakeups" is derived from system_server data; adb shell dumpsys activity, dumpsys window, dumpsys package each query a specific service.

Real-life picture. A city hall with departments (licences, roads, water). Citizens (apps) never enter the back office; they speak at the counter (Binder proxy).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying AMS is in the app process or part of ActivityManager in your process.
  • Forgetting that system_server is a single point of failure.
  • Confusing ATMS (Activities) and AMS (processes, services) after Android 10.

notes.title: App process spawn path
notes.html:
What it is. The chain of events from "user taps your icon" to "your Application.onCreate runs".

Steps.

  1. Launcher (itself an app) calls startActivity -> Binder -> ATMS in system_server.
  2. ATMS sees the target has no running process. AMS asks ZygoteProcess to start it: writes arguments (uid, gid, seinfo, abi, nice-name, target SDK, runtime flags) over the Zygote socket.
  3. Zygote forks; the child specializes (SELinux, uid, seccomp), maps the APK, sets up the class loader path.
  4. Child runs RuntimeInit -> ActivityThread.main(): creates the main Looper, then attach() calls IActivityManager.attachApplication(IApplicationThread) back to AMS.
  5. AMS replies with bindApplication(...) (app info, instrumentation, compat info); handleBindApplication creates the PathClassLoader, LoadedApk, the Application object, installs ContentProviders (installContentProviders, which run before Application.onCreate) and then calls Application.onCreate().
  6. AMS tells the app to scheduleLaunchActivity -> handleLaunchActivity -> Activity.onCreate/onStart/onResume; first frame drawn when the ViewRoot finishes traversal ("Displayed" time in logcat).
Launcher -> ATMS -> AMS -> Zygote(fork) -> ActivityThread.main -> attachApplication
        -> bindApplication -> ContentProviders.onCreate -> Application.onCreate -> Activity.onCreate -> first frame

Cold vs warm vs hot. Cold: process created (all steps). Warm: process alive but Activity recreated. Hot: Activity brought to front. Startup metrics: adb shell am start -W, "Displayed" logcat line, ApplicationStartInfo (API 35), Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric.

Real examples. Libraries that auto-init through ContentProvider (older Firebase, WorkManager before App Startup, LeakCanary) add time before Application.onCreate; Jetpack App Startup consolidates them into one provider.

Real-life picture. Opening a shop in the morning: the landlord (system) copies the keys (fork), you arrive, sign in with the security desk (attach), then the lights are switched on (providers), then the till opens (Application.onCreate).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Application.onCreate runs before ContentProviders; providers run first.
  • Forgetting that the process is created even for a broadcast or service start.
  • Treating the launcher as part of the OS rather than an ordinary app.

notes.title: USAP pool and per-app preloading
notes.html:
What it is. Two refinements to the Zygote model. USAP (Unspecialized App Process, Android 10) keeps a pool of already-forked, not-yet-specialized processes so that app start skips the fork cost and the socket round-trip. An app zygote (Android 10, android:zygotePreloadName) is a per-app (or per-UID) zygote used by isolated services, so heavy app-specific preloading (e.g. a WebView or media renderer's libraries) happens once and isolated child processes are forked from it.

Mechanism. USAP: Zygote pre-forks a small pool (persist.device_config.runtime_native.usap_pool_enabled; default pool around 10 on devices where it is enabled) and the system picks one, sends specialization data, and the process finishes specializing as the app. The pool refills in the background. It cuts several ms of start latency but costs memory for idle processes, so it is tuned per device. App zygote: declared by <service android:isolatedProcess="true" android:useAppZygote="true"> with a ZygotePreload class; isolated processes have no permissions and a unique UID, so a shared preload parent speeds them up without weakening isolation.

Real examples. Chromium/WebView renderers use isolated processes (with an app zygote on Android 10+ to preload native libs, reducing renderer startup). Pixel devices advertise faster app starts partly via USAP.

Real-life picture. A taxi stand with engines already running and drivers waiting in line (USAP), so a passenger hops in without waiting for the car to warm up.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing USAP is an app-level feature. It is platform-level.
  • Confusing the app zygote with the main Zygote.
  • Forgetting isolated processes cannot access most resources.

notes.title: DEX and multidex
notes.html:
What it is. The Android runtime does not run .class files; the build converts them to DEX (Dalvik Executable) files, which are more compact. A single DEX file can reference at most 65,536 methods (a 16-bit index in the method reference table), and likewise fields and types.

Mechanism. D8 compiles .class -> classes.dex (R8 additionally shrinks/optimizes). When the app exceeds 64K method references (counting references including library methods, not only your own), the build must emit classes2.dex, classes3.dex, ... This is multidex.

  • API 21+ (ART): native support; ART loads all classesN.dex files at install time and compiles them to OAT; no extra library.
  • API 20 and below (Dalvik): needs androidx.multidex:multidex and MultiDexApplication (or MultiDex.install(this) in attachBaseContext); only classes.dex is loaded at start and the rest are injected into the class loader; the main dex must contain classes needed at startup, otherwise NoClassDefFoundError at launch.

Spot-the-bug. Build error Cannot fit requested classes in a single dex file (# methods: 70000 > 65536) or a runtime crash on Android 4.x with ClassNotFoundException for a class needed in Application.onCreate: the class was not in the main dex. Fix: multiDexEnabled true, set multiDexKeepFile/multiDexKeepProguard (legacy), reduce methods (R8, remove unused SDKs, avoid pulling huge libraries like Guava full), use minSdk 21+ to drop legacy multidex.

Performance note. More DEX files means larger install-time dexopt and, on old devices, a slower cold start; R8 in full mode and baseline profiles mitigate it. Count methods with ./gradlew :app:dependencies and the APK Analyzer (Android Studio) which shows DEX method counts per package.

Real examples. Large apps (Facebook famously hit the limit early and built their own "dex loader" tricks; Uber and Airbnb ship 5-10+ dex files); Google Play services split by modules partly to avoid method count growth.

Real-life picture. A phone book with a maximum of 65,536 lines per volume: when you have more contacts you simply start volume 2, but on old phones the reader only opened volume 1 at the start.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting only your own methods; referenced library methods count too.
  • Saying multidex needs a library on all versions. API 21+ is native.
  • Forgetting the main-dex keep rules on Dalvik-era devices.
  • Believing R8 never changes the DEX count.

notes.title: APK vs AAB
notes.html:
What it is. An APK is the installable package (a zip with DEX, resources, native libraries, manifest, signature). An Android App Bundle (AAB) is a publishing format you upload to Google Play; Play uses it to generate optimized APKs per device (split APKs). You cannot install an AAB directly (use bundletool for local tests).

Mechanism. The AAB has base/ plus optional feature modules (dist:module), with all ABIs, densities and languages. Google Play's Dynamic Delivery builds: a base APK, and config splits for the device ABI, screen density and language (split_config.arm64_v8a.apk, split_config.xxhdpi.apk, split_config.en.apk), plus on-demand/conditional/instant feature modules. Play signs the generated APKs with the app signing key (Play App Signing; you hold only an upload key). Typical downloads are 15-20% (sometimes more) smaller.

my-app.aab
 |- base/ (dex, manifest, res, lib/arm64-v8a, lib/x86_64 ...)
 |- feature_camera/
 -> Play serves: base.apk + split_config.arm64_v8a.apk + split_config.xxhdpi.apk + split_config.hi.apk

Consequences.

  • Since August 2021 new apps on Play must be AABs.
  • Because the final APK differs per device, ABI/density/language splits can cause bugs: e.g. a locale not downloaded after a runtime language switch (use SplitCompat/languages handling and Play Core / Play Feature Delivery APIs), resources missing on-device, lib extraction differences.
  • Sideloading AAB output requires bundletool build-apks --connected-device or universal APK mode.
  • Android 13+ platform: App Bundle features pair with install-time vs on-demand modules; sizes limited (base 200 MB, total download 4 GB for AAB uploads, confirm current Play limits).
  • Alternative stores (Samsung, Huawei, F-Droid) may still require APKs, so many teams build both.

Real examples. Spotify, Netflix, Uber use AAB; Duolingo and games use on-demand modules (asset delivery) for levels; Google Maps offline language packs via splits.

Real-life picture. A tailor with a full pattern book (AAB) who cuts and sews a suit in your exact size (APK) rather than handing out one huge one-size-fits-all garment.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the AAB is installed on the device.
  • Forgetting upload key vs app signing key.
  • Missing locale/density splits when testing only a universal APK.
  • Confusing instant apps and on-demand modules.

notes.title: ART execution modes
notes.html:
What it is. ART can run your code in three ways, and modern Android mixes them: interpret it (slow start-up friendly, no compile), JIT compile hot methods at runtime, or run AOT (ahead-of-time) compiled native code from an OAT file.

Timeline of ART versions.

  • Android 4.4: Dalvik JIT default; ART optional.
  • Android 5-6 (API 21-23): full AOT at install (slow installs, big OTA updates).
  • Android 7 (API 24)+: hybrid: interpreter + JIT + profile-guided AOT. App installs fast (no full compile), runs interpreted/JIT at first, records a profile of hot methods, and a background dex2oat job (idle and charging, bg-dexopt) compiles only the profiled hot code.
  • Android 8 (API 26)+: vdex files (verified dex), compiler filters tweaks; Android 9+ cloud profiles (Play delivers aggregated profiles); Android 12 adds ART module updates via Mainline (ART updatable without full OTA); Android 10 adds a boot image profile update path.
install -> verify (vdex) only
run 1..N -> interpreter -> JIT hot methods -> profile saved (/data/misc/profiles)
idle+charging -> dex2oat compiles profiled methods (speed-profile) -> .odex/.art/.vdex
next launches -> mostly AOT code, fast

Why hybrid. Full AOT wasted storage and made updates slow; pure JIT started slowly each launch and used CPU/RAM. Hybrid compiles what users actually run.

Real examples. The first launches of a freshly installed Instagram or Maps are slower than later ones; that gap is what Baseline Profiles close. Play Store "Cloud Profiles" help first-time users.

Real-life picture. A chef who reads the recipe each time at first (interpreting), then notices which dishes sell most and prepares those in advance during quiet hours (AOT).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying ART always compiles everything at install (only 5-6 did).
  • Forgetting JIT is part of ART.
  • Not mentioning the profile and idle-time dexopt.
  • Mixing Dalvik's JIT (trace-based, no persistent cache) with ART's.

notes.title: Install-time dexopt and compile filters and profiles
notes.html:
What it is. The compile step (dex2oat/dexopt) can run in different compiler filters that trade install time, storage and speed. Profiles tell the compiler which methods matter.

Compiler filters (the common ones).

Filter What it compiles
verify verifies dex only, no native code (fast install, runs interpreted/JIT)
speed-profile compiles only methods listed in the profile (the default for installed apps)
speed compiles all methods (best speed, big OAT, slow dexopt)
everything compiles even non-startup methods; debugging
quicken (legacy, removed in Android 12) optimizes dex bytecode only
space, space-profile minimize size

Where profiles come from.

  1. Runtime profiles collected by JIT on the device.
  2. Cloud profiles (Play delivers aggregated profiles from other users, Android 9+).
  3. Baseline Profiles you ship: baseline-prof.txt in src/main, generated by the Macrobenchmark BaselineProfileRule (Jetpack androidx.baselineprofile Gradle plugin). AGP compiles it to assets/dexopt/baseline.prof. At install, Play or ProfileInstaller (for non-Play installs, runs on first launch) hands it to ART so the hot paths are AOT-compiled early. Startup Profiles additionally order classes in DEX for faster loading.

Measured effect. Google reports roughly 30% faster first-launch/startup for apps with baseline profiles (varies a lot; measure with Macrobenchmark CompilationMode.None() vs Partial()). Without profile, first launches after install run mostly in interpreter+JIT: slow cold start, janky scrolling on first use.

Cost/perf optimization scenario. App has slow first launch after install/update (updates also drop the compiled code; Play now re-applies). Actions: add Baseline Profile covering startup + critical journeys (scrolling feed, checkout), include libraries (Compose and AndroidX ship their own profiles), keep profileinstaller dependency, verify with adb shell dumpsys package dexopt (shows status speed-profile) and cmd package compile -m speed-profile -f <pkg>, compare cold start percentiles via Macrobenchmark and field metrics from Firebase Performance/Play Vitals. Watch the profile staleness as code changes: regenerate in CI each release.

Real examples. Google Chrome and Maps, Meta, Twitter, Duolingo report double-digit startup gains from Baseline Profiles; Jetpack Compose itself ships profiles inside the library AAR.

Real-life picture. A school timetable highlighting the lessons likely to come up in the exam: you revise only those in advance (compile), not the whole textbook.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming speed is the default (it is speed-profile).
  • Forgetting that profile effects need a release (non-debuggable) build.
  • Believing baseline profiles speed up the first frame only; they also improve jank in listed journeys.
  • Not regenerating profiles as code changes.

notes.title: Classloading
notes.html:
What it is. A class loader finds the bytes of a class by name and turns them into a usable class when first needed. On Android, your app code is loaded by a PathClassLoader that knows the paths of your APK's DEX files.

Mechanism. Hierarchy (parent-first delegation): BootClassLoader (framework/core libraries) <- PathClassLoader (app, created by LoadedApk) ; splits and shared libraries add DexPathList entries or child loaders. DexClassLoader loads dex/APK/jar from arbitrary paths (plugins). InMemoryDexClassLoader (API 26) loads from a buffer. loadClass(name) asks the parent first, then looks in its DexPathList.dexElements array in order; the first class found wins (which is why duplicate classes across modules cause hard-to-find bugs).

Class lifecycle. Load -> Link (verify, prepare) -> Initialize (static initializers run on first use). With AOT/OAT, classes in the app image are resolved faster. Class initialization order issues: static init cycles can deadlock between threads; heavy static initializers slow first use; a failure leaves NoClassDefFoundError ("Could not initialize class X") for all later uses.

Production patterns. ClassNotFoundException/NoClassDefFoundError after R8 (missing keep rule for reflection), after Dynamic Feature split installation without SplitCompat, on Dalvik multidex (not in main dex), or duplicate library versions (Duplicate class build error vs silent runtime clash with plugins).

Real examples. Plugin systems (Tinder-style experiment frameworks, Alipay mini-programs, Tencent's Shadow) use DexClassLoader; Google Play Feature Delivery relies on SplitCompat to add split APKs to the class loader of the running app.

Real-life picture. A librarian who first asks the head librarian (parent), and only if the head does not have the book searches her own shelves, in order.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a child-first order. Default is parent-first.
  • Forgetting static initializers run lazily, not at load time.
  • Mixing DexClassLoader (needs an optimized dir pre-API 26) and PathClassLoader.
  • Ignoring duplicate class on classpath ordering.

notes.title: Hidden API restrictions
notes.html:
What it is. Android has public SDK APIs and many internal "hidden" methods/fields (marked @hide) that apps used via reflection. Since Android 9 (API 28) the platform restricts access to them, to keep apps from depending on internals that can change.

Mechanism. Lists: whitelist (SDK, allowed), greylist (restricted unless on a per-release exemption list, unsupported), blocklist (blocked, throws), and since Android 10 the grey lists are further sub-divided by max target SDK (greylist-max-o, max-p, max-q...). A reflective call (Class.forName, getDeclaredMethod, JNI GetMethodID) to a restricted member from an app targeting a version beyond the list's max throws NoSuchMethodException/NoSuchFieldException (or logs a warning in "just warn" mode). The check is in ART (hiddenapi flag per member in the DEX), based on the caller's class loader domain (platform vs app code).

Detect. Logcat tag hiddenapi shows Accessing hidden method Landroid/...;->foo()V (greylist, reflection, allowed). Static check: veridex tool, Android Studio lint, adb shell settings put global hidden_api_policy 1 to disable enforcement in debug (not a fix). Check also libraries (old Glide/Fresco/Xposed-style hacks, TextView reflection, accessing mFlags).

Production incident (reflection break). After bumping targetSdk, a legacy library that reflected into android.app.ActivityThread or Resources.mThemeImpl crashed only on some OS versions with NoSuchMethodError or silently stopped working; staged rollout shows crashes on one API level. Fix: update/replace the library, use the official API (there is usually a replacement: Display.getRealSize, WindowInsets), request a new public API through Google's issue tracker, or remove the feature; do not use "double reflection" or exemption hacks (VMRuntime.setHiddenApiExemptions via LSPosed-style tools), which are fragile and violate policy.

Real examples. Old versions of Facebook/Twitter SDKs, HTTP stacks touching HttpURLConnection internals, and rooted-device detection libraries all had to be fixed; Google keeps an exemption list per release and a published "Restrictions on non-SDK interfaces" page (confirm the current list there).

Real-life picture. A theatre that now keeps the backstage door locked; actors and audience can still use the main door (SDK), but sneaking in through the maintenance corridor (reflection) may get you stopped.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the restrictions apply to Java code compiled against hidden stubs only. They apply to reflection and JNI too.
  • Treating the greylist as permanent.
  • Using the debug exemption setting as a "fix".
  • Ignoring third-party SDKs when auditing.

notes.title: Desugaring and R8 full mode
notes.html:
What it is. Desugaring lets you use newer Java language features and APIs (lambdas, java.time, Stream, try-with-resources, default interface methods) on older Android versions by rewriting them at build time. R8 is the compiler (D8 + shrinker + optimizer + obfuscator) that also performs desugaring. R8 full mode is the stricter optimization mode (default in AGP 8.0+).

Mechanism. Language desugaring: D8 rewrites lambdas to synthetic classes (or invokedynamic lowered), default methods to static helper classes. Core library desugaring (coreLibraryDesugaringEnabled true + com.android.tools:desugar_jdk_libs) backports java.time, java.util.stream, etc. to API < 26 by shipping a rewritten library in your DEX (adds ~hundreds of KB, uses the j$. prefix). Production incident: a NoClassDefFoundError/NoSuchMethodError for java.time.* or java.util.stream.* on API 21-25 only, or a crash in a library compiled against desugared APIs when the app itself did not enable core library desugaring (the library needs the app to enable it); or a version mismatch of desugar_jdk_libs with AGP/D8.

R8 full mode (AGP 8.0+ default android.enableR8.fullMode=true). Differences from compat mode: stricter assumptions: no longer keeps default constructors for classes referenced only by Class.forName/reflection unless a keep rule says so; removes unused members of interfaces; stricter on Class.getDeclaredField use; optimizes generic signatures and annotations away unless kept (-keepattributes Signature,*Annotation*); changes more of the class hierarchy (vertical class merging, horizontal merging). Migration under live traffic: enable in a build first; run full UI tests against the release variant; scan usage.txt/seeds.txt/configuration.txt and the mapping file; add keep rules for reflection users (Gson models, Retrofit interfaces w/ Signature, Room/Moshi codegen are safe, DI frameworks, JNI callbacks); check libraries' consumer rules; upload mapping.txt to Crashlytics/Play; roll out via staged rollout watching crash-free rate, NoSuchMethodException, ClassCastException, JSON parse failures, ClassNotFoundException; keep the previous mode switch (android.enableR8.fullMode=false) for rollback within one release.

Real examples. Gson-based apps lose field names in full mode without @SerializedName or keep rules (JSON parses to nulls); Retrofit 2.9+ and OkHttp ship consumer rules; Square, Google and Meta use R8 full mode with large keep-rule audits.

Real-life picture. A strict editor who now cuts every sentence that no one visibly refers to, including ones that were only referenced through a side note (reflection) unless you highlight them.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing desugaring needs no library for java.time.
  • Testing R8 only on debug builds (minify is off there).
  • Forgetting to upload mapping files, making crashes unreadable.
  • Putting -dontwarn everywhere instead of fixing the missing class.

notes.title: APK signing and install verification
notes.html:
What it is. Every APK must be signed, so Android can check who made it and that it was not modified, and so updates come only from the same developer.

Mechanism and schemes.

  • v1 (JAR signing): signs each file in the APK individually (META-INF); an attacker could add files; slower to verify.
  • v2 (API 24) and v3 (API 28, supports key rotation with a proof-of-rotation lineage) and v4 (API 30, a separate .idsig file enabling incremental APK install for adb streaming): sign the whole APK file (APK Signing Block before the central directory). Any byte change breaks it. v3.1 (API 33) refines rotation for targeted SDK levels.
  • PackageManagerService verifies the signature at install; for updates the new APK's signing certificate must match the installed one (or be in the rotation lineage), else INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE. Same signature enables sharedUserId and signature-level permissions.
  • minSdk decides which scheme(s) are needed; v1 needed for minSdk < 24; AGP picks automatically. Apps targeting 30+ must use v2 or higher.

Play App Signing. Google holds the app signing key; you sign the AAB with an upload key. Benefits: key reset after loss, key upgrade. The App Links assetlinks.json must contain the app signing key fingerprint. Debug builds use the debug keystore, a different fingerprint (hence Google Sign-In/Firebase SHA-1 config mismatches).

Zipalign. For v1 only, align uncompressed data to 4 bytes; with v2+ sign after zipalign (apksigner does this order), otherwise the signature is broken.

Real examples. Banks and Play Integrity checks verify the signing certificate; Samsung/Xiaomi OTAs rely on same-signature updates; losing the old self-managed keystore (pre-Play App Signing) forced some apps to publish a new package name.

Real-life picture. A tamper-evident seal on a medicine box: the whole box is sealed (v2+), not each tablet strip (v1); open it and the seal tells everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying v1 protects the whole APK.
  • Re-signing after modifying the APK without zipalign order.
  • Using the upload key fingerprint where the app signing key is needed.
  • Thinking signing = encryption.

notes.title: system_server watchdog and failure modes
notes.html:
What it is. system_server contains a Watchdog thread that detects deadlocks or stalled key threads in the framework and kills system_server (causing a soft reboot) if they do not recover.

Mechanism. com.android.server.Watchdog registers monitors (Watchdog.Monitor, methods named monitor() that briefly take the service's main lock) for AMS, WMS, PMS, PowerManagerService, InputManagerService, and checks handler threads (foreground, UI, I/O, display, animation). Every 30 seconds (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT is 60 s in release, half-time warning at 30 s) it posts a check; if a monitor or handler does not respond within the timeout, it dumps stack traces (to /data/anr/ and dropbox, tag system_server_watchdog) and kills system_server with SIGKILL. Zygote notices its child died and restarts the whole Java framework, so the user sees the boot animation and all apps die.

Failure modes.

  • A service lock held while doing a slow operation (I/O, a Binder call to a stuck app/service, a synchronous call into a slow HAL): classic cause of "Watchdog: *** WATCHDOG KILLING SYSTEM PROCESS: Blocked in monitor com.android.server.am.ActivityManagerService".
  • Binder thread exhaustion in system_server (31 threads): all service threads busy waiting on one slow app.
  • Memory pressure, vendor driver hangs, storage stalls.

App-side relevance. Apps can contribute: very chatty or blocking Binder calls into system_server (e.g. synchronous provider queries holding system locks, large TransactionTooLarge storms, thousands of JobScheduler/alarm registrations, notification spam, huge PackageManager.getInstalledPackages calls) degrade it. Watchdog reboots appear in Play Vitals as device-level issues, not app crashes, and the ANR trace file for system_server names the blocked thread. Distinguish from app ANRs (Input dispatch 5 s, broadcast 10/60 s, service 20/200 s) handled by AMS/InputDispatcher, which are not Watchdog events.

Real examples. OEM bugs reported in AOSP issue tracker as "Watchdog: Blocked in handler on foreground thread"; Pixel bugreports with Watchdog: *** GOODBYE! lines; apps doing bindService loops against a crashing service have triggered ANRs, not Watchdog kills.

Real-life picture. A factory supervisor who rings a bell for every manager every 30 seconds; if one manager does not answer in time, the supervisor assumes the whole control room has frozen and restarts the factory.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing Watchdog kills with app ANRs.
  • Saying apps can crash system_server directly. They can only stress it.
  • Forgetting a system_server restart kills every app process.
  • Mixing up ANR timeouts.

notes.title: ABIs and native libraries
notes.html:
What it is. An ABI (Application Binary Interface) is the CPU instruction set your native (C/C++) code is compiled for: arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64, x86 (and riscv64 appearing in newer NDKs). A device picks the best ABI it supports.

Mechanism. Native libraries sit in lib/<abi>/libfoo.so inside the APK. At install, PackageManagerService (via NativeLibraryHelper) picks the primary ABI by comparing the device's supported ABIs (Build.SUPPORTED_ABIS, ordered) with the ABIs present in the APK, choosing one ABI folder and ignoring all others — it does not mix libraries from different ABIs. Spot-the-bug: the app ships arm64-v8a for its own library but a third-party SDK ships only armeabi-v7a. On arm64 devices, the system sees an arm64-v8a folder, picks 64-bit and does not load the SDK's 32-bit .so -> UnsatisfiedLinkError: dlopen failed: library "libsdk.so" not found only on 64-bit devices. Fix: ship all ABIs for all libraries, or restrict to the common set via ndk { abiFilters } (note emulators on x86 via translation). Play requires 64-bit support for native code (since August 2019 for new apps/updates), and Android 14+ devices drop 32-bit on some SoCs.

Other points.

  • android:extractNativeLibs="false" (AGP default for AAB/minSdk 23+): .so files stay uncompressed in the APK, are mmaped directly, saving install size and disk copies (needs page-aligned storage; and 16 KB page-size alignment is required for Android 15+ targets on 16 KB page devices; confirm Play deadlines).
  • Split by ABI via AAB: Play delivers only the device's ABI, shrinking downloads by ~30-40%.
  • System.loadLibrary("foo") loads libfoo.so and runs JNI_OnLoad; load failures happen late, at first use.
  • Houdini/ARM translation on x86 devices and Windows Subsystem for Android makes ABI checks in analytics messy.

Real examples. Games with Unity/Unreal shipping multiple ABIs; video apps with FFmpeg/ExoPlayer extensions; React Native / Flutter engines ship per-ABI libflutter.so; analytics SDKs with native crash handlers.

Real-life picture. Plugs for different countries: your charger must have the matching plug for the wall socket, and one country's plug type is chosen for the whole trip; mixing leftover adapters will not work.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the system picks per library. It picks one ABI for the whole app.
  • Shipping only 32-bit libs when the app also has a 64-bit lib.
  • Using abiFilters in debug and forgetting emulator ABIs.
  • Missing the 16 KB page alignment requirement for newer devices.

notes.title: Dynamic code loading
notes.html:
What it is. Loading code at runtime that was not part of the installed APK: Play Feature Delivery modules, plugin DEX files, downloaded JARs, or DexClassLoader.

Mechanism and rules.

  • Play Feature Delivery (sanctioned): on-demand modules installed via the Play Core / SplitInstallManager; with SplitCompat they join the app's class loader. Code is verified and signed by Play.
  • Self-downloaded code: DexClassLoader / InMemoryDexClassLoader. Google Play policy ("Device and Network Abuse") forbids updating or adding executable code outside Play (except interpreted JS in WebView and limited cases). Android 10 blocks executing files from app-writable locations with some exceptions (W^X for targetSdk 29+ for executable native code from the app data dir; for DEX, API 34 (Android 14) requires that dynamically loaded dex/jar files be read-only (setReadOnly()), otherwise SecurityException).
  • Security: verify signature/hash before loading; store in codeCacheDir / noBackupFilesDir; avoid world-writable paths; never load from external storage; code injection through a swapped file is full code execution in your app.

Migration under live traffic. Scenario: app uses a downloaded plugin DEX; targetSdk bump to 34 -> SecurityException: Writable dex file ... is not allowed. Steps: after writing the file call file.setReadOnly() before loading (and keep it read-only; re-download rather than rewrite), validate hash/signature, move to Play Feature Delivery where possible, ship a fallback code path, staged rollout, and monitor ClassNotFoundException/SecurityException rates and plugin load time; also check R8 interplay (plugin interface classes must be kept in host), and per-version compatibility between host and plugin (version negotiation).

Real examples. Mini-app platforms (WeChat, Paytm mini apps use JS/WebView rather than DEX), Google's Dynamic Features for large games, banks using Play Feature Delivery for rarely used flows, and Tinder/Firebase-style remote config (data only, not code).

Real-life picture. A kitchen that allows delivery of ingredients through the official supplier (Play) but forbids cooking food that a stranger leaves unchecked at the back door.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying downloading and executing code is fine if the file is yours; policy and OS rules block it.
  • Forgetting the read-only requirement on API 34.
  • Loading plugin code from external storage.
  • Not versioning the host/plugin contract.

notes.title: Build pipeline from source to installed code
notes.html:
What it is. The path your Kotlin file travels to become running code.

.kt/.java --kotlinc/javac--> .class
res/ + AndroidManifest --aapt2 compile/link--> resources.arsc, R class, binary XML
.class (+ libs, + desugaring) --R8 (D8 + shrink + optimize + obfuscate)--> classes.dex (classesN.dex)
native: CMake/ndk-build --> lib/<abi>/*.so
package: unsigned APK/AAB --zipalign--> --apksigner (v2/v3)--> signed APK
install: PMS verifies signature -> installd copies -> dex2oat (dexopt) --> .odex/.vdex/.art
run: Zygote fork -> PathClassLoader -> ART interpreter/JIT/AOT

Stages in detail.

  1. Compile: Kotlin/Java compilers produce .class; annotation processors/KSP generate code (Room, Hilt, Moshi).
  2. Resources: AAPT2 compiles XML/PNG into binary flat format, links into resources.arsc and R. Resource shrinking removes unused ones.
  3. Dex: D8 desugars and converts to DEX; R8 additionally shrinks, optimizes, obfuscates, and emits mapping.txt.
  4. Package and sign: APK zip or AAB (via bundletool); sign (v1-v4) after zipalign.
  5. Install (or Play delivers splits): PackageManagerService parses the manifest, verifies signature, installs, installd creates /data/data/<pkg>, dex2oat (profile-guided, verify or speed-profile) in the background or at install.
  6. Launch: see spawn path; baseline profile and cloud profile influence compilation.

Debugging by stage. Build errors (duplicate classes, 64K methods), merge conflicts in manifest (Merged Manifest tab), R8 missing class warnings, apkanalyzer, dexdump, javap for bytecode, aapt2 dump badging, bundletool dump manifest. Incremental installs: adb install streaming via v4 signature; Android Studio "Apply Changes" uses instrumentation to swap code.

Real examples. Google, Meta and Uber build pipelines add steps like bytecode instrumentation (ASM/Transform API replaced by AGP's AsmClassVisitorFactory), remote caching (Gradle build cache), and baseline profile generation in CI.

Real-life picture. A book printing line: write (compile), typeset (dex), shrink to a pocket edition (R8), bind and sign (APK), ship, and the bookshop (device) pre-marks the popular chapters (dexopt).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing R8 and ProGuard are separate in modern AGP (R8 reads ProGuard rules).
  • Signing before zipalign with v1-only tools.
  • Forgetting classes.dex is produced from .class, not .kt.
  • Not knowing where annotation processing happens.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Zygote preloads the framework once and forks each app (copy-on-write, shared memory); system_server is forked first and hosts AMS/ATMS/WMS/PMS.
  • Cold start: launcher -> ATMS/AMS -> Zygote fork -> ActivityThread.main -> bindApplication -> providers -> Application.onCreate -> Activity.
  • USAP pre-forks processes; app zygote speeds isolated processes.
  • DEX has a 64K method reference limit; API 21+ handles multidex natively.
  • AAB is a publishing format; Play creates per-device split APKs and signs them with the app signing key.
  • ART is hybrid: interpreter + JIT + profile-guided AOT; Baseline Profiles and cloud profiles precompile hot paths.
  • Class loading is parent-first; first found class wins; duplicates and missing keep rules cause runtime failures.
  • Hidden API restrictions block reflection into internals; use public APIs.
  • Desugaring and R8 full mode need core library desugaring and explicit keep rules; test release builds.
  • Signing v2/v3/v4 protects the whole APK; update needs the same cert; ABI folders are chosen as a whole.
  • Watchdog kills a blocked system_server; dynamic code loading is restricted (Play policy, read-only dex on API 34).

questions.promptHtml: What is Zygote, and why can an Android app process start so much faster than launching a fresh JVM-style process?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know that "app process" is a fork of a pre-warmed runtime, not a cold exec. It separates people who only use the SDK from people who understand the platform.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Zygote is a process that init starts at boot. It boots ART, preloads thousands of framework classes, resources and shared libraries, and then waits on a socket. When a new app process is needed, system_server asks Zygote to fork itself. The child inherits all that preloaded memory copy-on-write, so I don't pay for runtime startup or class loading of the framework. Only the app-specific specialisation (uid, SELinux context, then my APK's code) is left to do.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without Zygote, every app launch would: exec a runtime binary, initialise ART, load and verify ~thousands of android.* classes, load drawables and libandroid_runtime, libhwui etc. That is hundreds of ms and tens of MB of private memory per app.

Boot sequence (simplified):

init --(init.zygote64.rc)--> app_process --> ZygoteInit.main()
   preload(): preloaded-classes list, framework resources, shared libs, OpenGL, WebView bits
   forkSystemServer()  ---> system_server (AMS, ATMS, WMS, PMS ...)
   runSelectLoop()     <--- /dev/socket/zygote  (waits for fork requests)
                                  |
 system_server: "start process for com.foo.app" --- args over socket
                                  v
   Zygote.forkAndSpecialize(uid, gid, seinfo, nice-name, ...)
        parent: returns pid to system_server, goes back to loop
        child : drop privileges, set SELinux domain, seccomp, then
                RuntimeInit -> ActivityThread.main()

Key points:

  • fork() is copy-on-write: preloaded pages stay physically shared between all apps until written. That is why dumpsys meminfo shows big "Shared" numbers and why PSS divides them across processes.
  • Zygote itself must never run app code and must stay clean (no threads started, no heap mutation), otherwise forking a multi-threaded or dirty process is unsafe. Preloaded classes are initialised but app-specific state is not.
  • Devices usually have zygote (64-bit) and zygote_secondary (32-bit); the choice follows the app's primary ABI.
  • Special zygotes: the WebView zygote and, since API 29, an optional per-app "app zygote" for isolated services. API 29+ also has a pool of pre-forked unspecialised processes (see the USAP question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Inspect it on a device.

adb shell ps -A | grep -E "zygote|system_server"
adb shell cat /system/etc/preloaded-classes | wc -l
adb shell cat /proc/$(pidof system_server)/status | grep PPid   # parent is zygote

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Zygote "preloads my app". It preloads the framework only; your classes load after the fork.
  • Assuming static state in my app is shared with other apps. After the fork each app has its own copy of everything it writes.
  • Thinking the first launch after boot is as fast as later ones. Preloading cost is paid once at boot, not per app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the child still isolated from other apps? → After fork it gets its own uid, SELinux domain, seccomp filter and namespaces; sharing is only read-only copy-on-write pages.
  2. What happens if system_server dies? → Zygote gets killed with it and init restarts it, which restarts the whole Java framework (a "soft reboot"); all app processes go away.
  3. Why can't I preload my own app's classes into Zygote? → Zygote is a system process started from the system image; apps have no hook there. Only privileged OEM/partner code can add to preload lists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer is "it is the parent of all app processes and is faster". The senior answer explains copy-on-write sharing, why it affects PSS accounting, the clean-heap constraint, per-ABI zygotes, and that the work left after fork (bindApplication, class loading of my APK, ContentProviders, Application.onCreate) is the only part I control.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team was puzzled that their "30 MB" app looked like 60 MB in RSS. The shared Zygote pages counted in RSS but are split in PSS; they were comparing the wrong metric.

questions.promptHtml: What do ActivityManagerService, ActivityTaskManagerService, WindowManagerService and PackageManagerService each do? Where do they live and how does my app talk to them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every lifecycle bug, permission crash and window issue ends at one of these services. Interviewers want to see a mental map, not memorised names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: They are Java services running inside the system_server process. My app reaches them through Binder via Context.getSystemService or hidden managers. PackageManagerService knows what is installed and resolves intents and permissions. ActivityTaskManagerService, split out of ActivityManagerService in Android 10, owns activities, tasks and the back stack. ActivityManagerService now owns processes, services, broadcasts, providers, OOM adjustment and ANR handling. WindowManagerService owns windows, surfaces, insets, input focus and transitions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App process                              system_server
 ┌───────────────┐   Binder (IPC)    ┌────────────────────────────────┐
 │ ActivityThread│ <───────────────> │ ATMS  tasks, activities, back  │
 │ (main thread) │  ApplicationThread│       stack, launch modes      │
 │ Instrumentation  (callbacks into  │ AMS   processes, services,     │
 │ Context       │   app)            │       broadcasts, providers,   │
 └───────────────┘                   │       oom_adj, ANR             │
                                     │ WMS   windows, insets, focus,  │
                                     │       animations, input route  │
                                     │ PMS   APK scan, permissions,   │
                                     │       intent resolution, dexopt│
                                     └────────────────────────────────┘
  • The app never calls a lifecycle method on itself from the system's view: ATMS tells the app's ApplicationThread (a Binder object) to schedule a ClientTransaction (launch, resume, pause, destroy). ActivityThread posts it on the main Looper, and only then onCreate runs.
  • AMS tracks every process in ProcessRecord, computes its oom_adj, and tells lmkd (via ProcessList) what to kill first.
  • PMS reads /data/system/packages.xml and scans APKs at boot and install; queryIntentActivities, permission grants and signature checks are answered here. Package visibility filtering (API 30+) is applied in this layer.
  • WMS decides which window gets input and how insets are dispatched; SurfaceFlinger (a separate native process) composes the surfaces WMS describes.
  • Other services in the same process: InputManagerService, PowerManagerService, NotificationManagerService, JobScheduler, etc. A slow lock in one service can hurt callers of an unrelated service because they share the process and threads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys activity activities   # ATMS: tasks and activities
adb shell dumpsys activity processes    # AMS: ProcessRecords and oom_adj
adb shell dumpsys window windows        # WMS: windows and focus
adb shell dumpsys package com.foo.app   # PMS: permissions, signatures, dexopt state

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "AMS manages activities". True before Android 10; since then that is ATMS (in the com.android.server.wm package). Still correct as a system, but say it precisely.
  • Believing these are separate processes. They are all in system_server.
  • Forgetting that the app is also an IPC server (ApplicationThread), which is how the system pushes lifecycle callbacks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does SurfaceFlinger fit? → Separate native process; WMS tells it layers, SurfaceFlinger composites at vsync.
  2. Why does a slow startActivity sometimes hit the app? → The app's call is a synchronous Binder call into system_server; if its locks are contended, my main thread blocks (see the main-thread Binder section).
  3. How does a permission check on a Binder call work? → The service reads the caller's uid via Binder.getCallingUid() and checks it against PMS grants.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the four names. Senior knows the ATMS/AMS split, that lifecycle is a server-pushed ClientTransaction, can name the matching dumpsys command for each, and ties it to real debugging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "background launch blocked" bug was diagnosed in minutes by reading dumpsys activity activities plus the ATMS log line that gave the exact background-activity-start reason.

questions.promptHtml: What is a DEX file, and what is the 64K method limit? When do I need multidex today?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic fundamentals question that also reveals whether you know that the answer changed when ART replaced Dalvik.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android runs DEX bytecode, not JVM .class files. D8 converts and merges classes into classes.dex. A single DEX can reference at most 65,536 methods because method IDs are indexed with 16 bits. Past that you get multiple DEX files (classes2.dex ...). On minSdk 21 and above ART supports multiple DEX files natively, so I just enable it, no library. Below 21, Dalvik only loads the main DEX and I need the androidx.multidex library.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pipeline: Kotlin/Java → .class → D8 (desugar + convert) or R8 (shrink + optimise + D8) → one or more .dex inside the APK.
  • The limit is not "65,536 methods you wrote". It is method references in the DEX method_ids table, which includes methods you call in libraries (String.length() counts as one reference). Field references have the same 16-bit limit.
  • Build error if exceeded and multidex is off: Cannot fit requested classes in a single dex file (# methods: 67345 > 65536).
  • minSdk 21+: ART's boot loads every classesN.dex listed in the APK. AGP enables multidex automatically for minSdk 21+; no code needed.
  • minSdk < 21 ("legacy multidex"): Dalvik loads only classes.dex at start. MultiDexApplication (or MultiDex.install(base) in attachBaseContext) loads the rest. Classes needed before that point must be in the main dex (computed by D8 from the keep rules; extra ones via multiDexKeepFile/multiDexKeepProguard).
  • Shrinking with R8 and splitting by feature (dynamic features) are better than relying on multidex to hide a growing method count.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts (module) - only needed when minSdk < 21 for the runtime lib
android {
    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 21          // multidex native, no extra lib needed
        multiDexEnabled = true
    }
}
dependencies {
    // implementation("androidx.multidex:multidex:2.0.1")   // only for minSdk < 21
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Multidex slows down every app on every device". On ART it is nearly free; legacy multidex costs install-time extraction and first-launch time on Dalvik.
  • Reading the limit as classes, not method references.
  • Putting a heavily used class in a secondary dex on legacy multidex and touching it before MultiDex.install runs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does R8 reduce the count? → Yes; tree-shaking removes unused methods, which is the first thing to try.
  2. Does each library count? → Yes, their referenced methods count after shrinking; check with apkanalyzer dex references app.apk or Android Studio's APK Analyzer.
  3. Why can legacy multidex produce NoClassDefFoundError at startup only on old devices? → A class in a secondary dex referenced before install() ran; fix with keep rules for the main dex.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "64K limit, enable multidex." Senior explains method references, the 16-bit index origin, ART vs Dalvik loading, main dex lists for legacy, and treats method count as something to shrink and split, not just tolerate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dependency upgrade pushed the app past 65,536 on a minSdk-19 flavour. The release build passed CI (minSdk 24 debug) but the legacy flavour crashed in Application.onCreate on one cohort. See the scenario on this later in the chunk.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an APK and an Android App Bundle? What actually gets installed on a user's phone from the Play Store?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests that you understand build artifacts and why a debug APK on a QA phone can behave differently from what production users get.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An APK is the installable file. An AAB is a publishing format that Play cannot install directly. Play takes my AAB and generates split APKs per device: a base APK plus config splits for ABI, screen density and language, and any dynamic feature modules. The user installs only what their device needs, signed with the Play app signing key. So the artifact I test locally may not be byte-identical to what ships.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AAB (upload, signed with upload key)
   base/  feature_x/  BundleConfig.pb  metadata/
        |  Play: bundletool-style split + re-sign with app signing key
        v
 Device receives:
   base.apk                 (code, shared resources, manifest)
   split_config.arm64_v8a   (native libs for this ABI only)
   split_config.xxhdpi      (density resources)
   split_config.en          (language)
   [feature_x.apk]          (on-demand / install-time modules)
  • Installed via PackageInstaller sessions: the splits belong to one package, share a uid and are verified together (needs Android 5.0 / API 21 for split APKs).
  • Benefits: smaller download (native libs and densities you do not need are excluded), dynamic feature delivery, and Play-side optimisations such as applying cloud profiles at install.
  • Gotchas: language splits mean the app must not assume every locale resource is present when you change locale at runtime (Play Core / SplitCompat or the per-app language APIs handle this); asset packs and feature modules need SplitCompat for access.
  • Local testing: bundletool build-apks --bundle=app.aab --connected-device then install-apks, or the --mode=universal option for a single APK. Android Studio's "Run" on an AAB-based config does this for you.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
bundletool build-apks --bundle=app.aab --output=app.apks --connected-device \
    --ks=release.jks --ks-key-alias=upload
bundletool install-apks --apks=app.apks

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only a universal debug APK and missing split-related bugs (missing ABI lib, missing language resources).
  • Thinking AAB makes the app smaller on disk for every device. It reduces download and install size relative to the universal APK; savings vary by device mix.
  • Confusing the upload key and the app signing key; users get an APK signed by the latter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I sideload an AAB? → No; produce APK sets with bundletool.
  2. What is the upload key for? → Authenticates my upload to Play; Play re-signs with the app signing key, which I cannot rotate casually.
  3. What goes wrong with native libs? → The device gets only its ABI split; a lib missing for that ABI crashes only for that device group (see the ABI scenario).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows AAB is "required by Play and smaller". Senior knows the split model, signing consequences, how to reproduce the exact split set locally, and what assumptions break (ABI, locale, feature module access).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crashes reported only from Play installs and not by QA on universal APKs were traced to a language split that did not contain a string override the QA build included.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through everything that happens, from the user tapping my app's icon to Activity.onCreate, for a cold start. Which parts run in which process?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cold start is the performance metric interviewers care about; this checks you can name every stage you can and cannot control.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The launcher calls startActivity, which is a Binder call into ATMS in system_server. ATMS sees no process for my package, so AMS asks Zygote over its socket to fork one. The child specialises (uid, SELinux), runs ActivityThread.main, creates the main Looper and calls back to AMS with attachApplication. AMS replies with bindApplication, which loads my APK, creates the Application, installs ContentProviders, runs Application.onCreate. Then ATMS schedules the launch transaction and Activity.onCreate runs, followed by first frame.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Launcher      system_server                 Zygote            New app process
   | startActivity (Binder) |                                       |
   |----------------------->| ATMS resolves intent (PMS), no process|
   |                        | AMS ProcessList.start --socket------->| fork + specialise
   |                        |                                       | ActivityThread.main()
   |                        |<----------- attachApplication --------| Looper.prepareMainLooper
   |                        |--- bindApplication ------------------>| handleBindApplication:
   |                        |                                       |  LoadedApk + ClassLoader
   |                        |                                       |  AppComponentFactory
   |                        |                                       |  ContentProviders.onCreate
   |                        |                                       |  Application.onCreate
   |                        |--- LaunchActivityItem (transaction)-->| Activity.onCreate/Start/Resume
   |                        | WMS shows starting window (splash)    | first draw -> "displayed"

What I control: everything from bindApplication onwards (provider init, Application.onCreate, Activity.onCreate, first-frame work). What I do not: process fork and the starting window, though the splash/theme affects perceived time.

Order inside the app process matters: Application.attachBaseContext → ContentProvider onCreate (all of them, including Jetpack App Startup initializers and library providers) → Application.onCreate → Activity. So library initialisation hidden in providers runs before my Application.onCreate.

Cold vs warm vs hot: cold = no process; warm = process alive but Activity must be recreated; hot = Activity just brought to front. Timeline numbers: Displayed in logcat | grep Displayed (the ActivityTaskManager line) and reportFullyDrawn for the app-defined end.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell am start -W -n com.foo.app/.MainActivity
# ThisTime / TotalTime / WaitTime; TotalTime includes process start for cold
adb shell am force-stop com.foo.app    # guarantees next launch is cold

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Application.onCreate runs first. Providers run before it.
  • Forgetting that the user sees the starting window early, so "time to first frame" ≠ "time since tap".
  • Measuring "cold start" after adb install -r without noting dexopt state (see the profile scenarios).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Application.attachBaseContext fit? → Right after the Application object is created, before providers; good place for multidex or crash reporter set-up.
  2. What does android:process change? → That process gets its own fork and its own Application.onCreate run.
  3. How is ActivityThread different from Activity? → ActivityThread is the per-process runtime driving the main Looper and executing system-pushed transactions; Activities are objects it manages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Zygote forks, Application.onCreate, then Activity". Senior draws the Binder round trips (attachApplication/bindApplication), names providers before Application, separates controllable from uncontrollable time, and knows am start -W semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cold start regression of 220 ms was a new analytics SDK that auto-initialised through a ContentProvider, invisible in Application.onCreate but obvious in a trace of handleBindApplication.

questions.promptHtml: How does ART execute my code? Explain interpreter, JIT, AOT and profile-guided compilation, and how that changed from Dalvik to now.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It exposes whether you understand why the same APK is slower right after install and faster later, which underpins every startup optimisation conversation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dalvik (pre-5.0) interpreted and later had a JIT. Android 5 switched to ART with full AOT compilation at install, which made installs slow and big. Android 7 moved to a hybrid: start interpreting, JIT hot code while running, record what was hot in a profile, then compile only that profile ahead-of-time while the device is idle and charging. Since then, profiles can also come from outside the device, from Play cloud profiles and from Baseline Profiles I ship, so new installs start with the hot paths already compiled.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Era Strategy Consequence
Dalvik (≤4.x) Interpreter, trace JIT (2.2+) Slow, code not persisted
ART, Android 5-6 Full AOT at install Long installs and OTAs, large oat files
ART, Android 7+ Interpreter + JIT + profile-guided AOT Fast installs; steady state improves after background dexopt
Android 9+ Cloud profiles from Play, plus (Jetpack) Baseline Profiles Better first-run performance
Android 12+ ART delivered as a Mainline (APEX) module Runtime improvements ship without full OTA

Runtime flow today:

  1. Code runs in the interpreter (a fast assembly interpreter in recent releases, called nterp in AOSP; I'd say "verify" on exact version).
  2. Methods crossing a hotness threshold are queued for the JIT, which compiles to machine code held in the JIT code cache.
  3. Hot methods and classes are recorded in a profile (/data/misc/profiles/cur/0/<pkg>/primary.prof). Profile data is merged into a reference profile.
  4. When the device is idle and charging, the bg-dexopt job (dex2oat) compiles methods listed in the profile with the speed-profile filter. Next launch runs AOT code for those paths.
  5. Classes failing verification at compile time fall back to the interpreter, which is slower; that is one reason startup can stay slow.

Why it matters: a freshly installed app, with no profile, runs mostly interpreted/JIT; first launches are slower and janky. This is what profiles pre-seed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell cmd package compile -m speed-profile -f com.foo.app   # force profile compile
adb shell cmd package compile -m speed -f com.foo.app           # compile everything
adb shell dumpsys package dexopt | grep -A3 com.foo.app          # current state

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "ART is AOT" only. That was true on 5-6; today it is mixed.
  • Benchmarking after a fresh adb install and calling the app slow. The profile is not built yet.
  • Believing JIT is disabled on ART. It is on; it feeds the profile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not AOT-compile everything again? → Install time, storage, RAM (larger oat files), and OTA time; profile-guided keeps the useful subset.
  2. Where does the .oat/.vdex/.art family fit? → Output of dex2oat per APK (covered in the install/dexopt question).
  3. How does that change release engineering? → Ship a Baseline Profile and measure startup with a realistic compilation mode.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "ART compiles at install". Senior gives the timeline, the profile loop, the idle/charging job, and links it to why first-run performance differs and how profiles fix it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After switching from a debug-like benchmark to CompilationMode.None vs Partial comparisons, a team found their "regression" was only missing profile data, not slower code.

questions.subtopic: Install-time dexopt, compile filters and profiles
questions.promptHtml: What happens to my APK's DEX at install time? What are compile filters, and where do Baseline Profiles and Play cloud profiles come in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the connection between build artifacts, the installer and runtime performance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When the package is installed, PackageManager runs dex2oat with a compile filter. Plain installs usually only verify the DEX (verify), leaving code to be interpreted and JIT'd. If the install includes a profile, such as my Baseline Profile or a Play cloud profile, the installer can compile the listed methods ahead of time with speed-profile. Later, the idle/charging bg-dexopt job refines it from the device's own usage profile.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Artifacts per package under /data/app/.../oat/<isa>/: base.vdex (verified DEX), base.odex (compiled code, optional), base.art (app image of preloaded classes, optional). These are produced by dex2oat.
  • Common compile filters (from least to most compile): verify (no native code), speed-profile (compile methods named in the profile), speed (compile all), everything. Older docs also show quicken; I'd say verify on current releases, as it was dropped in later versions.
  • Compilation reasons shown by dumpsys package dexopt: install, bg-dexopt, first-boot, ab-ota, cmdline, etc.
  • Baseline Profile: a human/Macrobenchmark-generated list of classes and methods (baseline-prof.txt) packaged in the APK/AAB as assets/dexopt/baseline.prof. At install, Play and system compile with it (Android 9+ via Play; on other installs ProfileInstaller library installs it on first run). Practice and generation belong to A6.
  • Cloud profiles: Play aggregates hot-method data from users who opted in, and ships it with updates so later installers get a profile on day one.
  • Dex Metadata (.dm) files carry the profile into the installer.
Install (Play)  --base.apk + .dm profile--> dex2oat --speed-profile--> .odex/.vdex
Run             --interpreter/JIT--> primary.prof
Idle+charging   --bg-dexopt--> merge profiles, recompile with speed-profile

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts - consumers outside Play still get the profile installed at first launch
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.profileinstaller:profileinstaller:1.3.1")
}
adb shell dumpsys package com.foo.app | grep -A4 "Dexopt state"
adb shell cmd package compile -m speed-profile -f com.foo.app

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming install always AOT-compiles. Most plain adb installs only verify.
  • Shipping a Baseline Profile but also stripping profileinstaller and sideloading; profile never applies.
  • Regenerating profiles rarely; code changes make stale rules ineffective.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the profile live on device? → Under /data/misc/profiles (cur and ref) on user builds, not accessible without root.
  2. Why does the first launch after an app update sometimes feel slow? → The old compiled code is invalid for the new APK; you restart from verify plus any shipped profile.
  3. Does a Baseline Profile help warm start? → Mostly cold start and first-use jank; warm paths are already JIT'd.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Baseline Profiles improve startup." Senior explains install-time filter, .dm, bg-dexopt, cloud profile, which installs get nothing, and how to verify with dumpsys package rather than guessing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same release was 30% slower on first launch for sideloaded enterprise installs than for Play installs; the fix was bundling profileinstaller so the profile was applied on those devices too.

questions.promptHtml: How does class loading work on Android? What is PathClassLoader, how does it find a class across multiple DEX files, and what goes wrong with duplicate classes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Duplicate-class, NoClassDefFoundError and ClassNotFoundException bugs are real production problems, and the answer requires knowing the loader chain.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: My app's code is loaded by a PathClassLoader (a BaseDexClassLoader) whose parent is the boot class loader. It holds a DexPathList with an ordered array of dex elements. A lookup asks the parent first, then walks classes.dex, classes2.dex, ... in order and returns the first match. So if two libraries bundle the same class, whichever dex comes first wins, silently. Classes are loaded lazily on first use, then verified and initialised.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
BootClassLoader  (framework: android.*, java.*)
        ^ parent
 PathClassLoader  -> DexPathList.dexElements = [ base.apk!classes.dex,
                                                  base.apk!classes2.dex,
                                                  split_*.apk ... ]
        loadClass(name):
          1. already loaded? return
          2. parent.loadClass(name)      // framework wins over app copies
          3. findClass: for each element -> dex.findClassDef(name)
  • Parent delegation means my app cannot shadow android.* or java.* classes. Shadowing app-level classes between libraries is possible via ordering.
  • Class lifecycle: load (find the DEX bytes) → link (verify bytecode, prepare statics) → initialise (<clinit>, run on first use). Static initialisers therefore run lazily, which affects startup order and class-init deadlocks.
  • ART verifies at dexopt time when it can. A class that fails verification is marked and always interpreted (slower); it throws VerifyError only if it truly cannot be used.
  • ClassNotFoundException (reflective Class.forName/loadClass) vs NoClassDefFoundError (a class existed at compile time but failed to load or initialise, including a failed <clinit>; the second access after a failed static init always yields NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class).
  • Dynamic features and split APKs add their own class loaders (a split class loader chained to the base loader).
  • Custom loaders: DexClassLoader loads dex from a path; plugin frameworks, and tools such as Instant Run formerly, use it. Platform restrictions apply (see the Android 14 scenario).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun describeLoader() {
    var cl: ClassLoader? = Foo::class.java.classLoader
    while (cl != null) {
        println(cl)            // dalvik.system.PathClassLoader[DexPathList[[zip file "/data/app/.../base.apk"]...
        cl = cl.parent
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating NoClassDefFoundError as "class missing from APK". Often it is a failed static init earlier; read the first exception in the log.
  • Shipping two versions of one library (e.g. via different transitive paths) and getting "works on my build"; Gradle resolution, not the runtime, should decide.
  • Doing heavy work in <clinit> of a class used on startup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the same class load twice? → Yes, in two loaders; they are different types (ClassCastException between "identical" classes).
  2. How do I find duplicates? → ./gradlew :app:dependencies, Lint/AGP duplicate-class checks (checkDuplicateClasses task), APK Analyzer.
  3. Why does Hilt/Dagger code not need reflection at runtime? → Generated code avoids reflective class lookup, which also makes it R8-friendly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ClassLoader loads classes." Senior explains the chain, dex ordering, load/link/init separation, the failed <clinit> rule, and how to diagnose duplicates at build time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK shaded an older okio copy; a rare dex-order change after adding a module made the old copy win and crashed one network path. checkDuplicateClasses in CI would have caught it.

questions.promptHtml: What are hidden API restrictions? How do they affect reflection and direct linking, and how do I find out if my app or a library is affected?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many apps and SDKs use reflection into android.* internals. The question tests knowledge of a major platform-compat mechanism and how to proactively test for it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Android 9 (API 28) the platform limits access to non-SDK interfaces: methods and fields that exist in the framework but are not in the public SDK. They are sorted into lists: SDK (allowed), unsupported (conditionally allowed), and blocked. Restrictions apply through reflection, JNI and direct linking, to all apps regardless of targetSdk, though the "unsupported" lists graduate to blocked with each release depending on targetSdk. Violations throw NoSuchMethodException/NoSuchFieldException or print warnings. I check with StrictMode.detectNonSdkApiUsage() and the veridex tool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The lists live in AOSP (hiddenapi-flags.csv / hiddenapi-unsupported.txt etc.). Classification: public (SDK), unsupported (greylist, accessible in the current release but may be restricted later, often only for apps targeting a newer SDK), max-target-X (accessible only while targetSdk ≤ X), blocked (always denied).
  • Mechanism: ART checks at the point of resolution (field/method lookup, JNI GetMethodID, linking), based on the caller's class loader (framework vs app domain). Calls from framework code are always allowed.
  • Failure shape: reflective lookup throws NoSuchMethodException; direct non-reflective use of a hidden method resolves as missing and fails at link time with NoSuchMethodError.
  • Warnings appear in logcat with a Accessing hidden method ... (unsupported, reflection, allowed) message when access is allowed but flagged.
  • Detection: StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder().detectNonSdkApiUsage() (API 28+) logs/penalises accessed non-SDK members at runtime; veridex scans an APK statically (including libraries) and reports hidden API use and which list they are in.
  • "Bypass" libraries that exploit meta-reflection exist. They are version-brittle and policy-risky; I would not ship one without a fallback.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Debug builds only: log non-SDK API usage
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG && Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.P) {
    StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
        StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder()
            .detectNonSdkApiUsage()
            .penaltyLog()
            .build()
    )
}
// Safe pattern for a reflective optimisation: tolerate failure and fall back
fun tryFastPath(): Boolean = try {
    val m = Class.forName("android.view.View").getDeclaredMethod("someHiddenMethod")
    m.isAccessible = true
    true
} catch (e: ReflectiveOperationException) {
    false   // blocked or removed on this OS; use public API path
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "it worked on API 28 so it works forever". Lists tighten each release; test on the newest preview.
  • Only checking my code; libraries (image loaders, ad SDKs, analytics) are the usual offenders.
  • Catching only NoSuchMethodException and not NoSuchFieldException/NoSuchMethodError at link time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does targetSdk change anything? → For max-target-X members yes (gone once targetSdk exceeds X); blocked members are denied regardless.
  2. Can I request a public API? → Yes, Google runs a process via the issue tracker for needed non-SDK APIs.
  3. Does R8 interact? → R8 rules can keep reflective members of my code, but cannot restore access to framework-hidden members.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Reflection on private APIs is blocked." Senior knows the list taxonomy, link/JNI/reflection vectors, targetSdk interplay, and the detection workflow in CI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A vendor SDK read a private field of ViewRootImpl; crashes appeared only on newer OS versions as list entries were tightened.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app supports minSdk 19 for a regional market (6% of 2.1M DAU, mostly low-end devices). A dependency bump pushes method references from 63,800 to 69,200. CI builds fine, because the debug variant uses minSdk 24 via a dev flavour. Release crash rate for the Android 4.4 cohort jumps from 0.3% to 11% right after rollout. Crashlytics shows:

java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/foo/di/AppGraph;
    at com.foo.App.onCreate(App.java:41)
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: Didn't find class "com.foo.di.AppGraph" on path: DexPathList[[zip file "/data/app/com.foo-1.apk"],nativeLibraryDirectories=[/system/lib]]
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {           // MultiDex.install is NOT called anywhere
        super.onCreate()
        AppGraph.init(this)              // lives in classes2.dex after the bump
    }
}

multiDexEnabled = true is set in defaultConfig.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the crash, fix it for the old cohort, and tell me why CI did not catch it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add ProGuard rules" or "increase minSdk" without noticing that the install step is missing. They may blame the library bump itself, or not realise the crash is limited to API < 21 because ART loads all dex files natively.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the crash only on API < 21? (confirms Dalvik legacy multidex). What does App extend? Which AGP/R8 version (does it generate the main-dex list)? Does the debug flavour differ in minSdk? How many devices still on 4.4 matter to the business?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at its current percentage. If the cohort is a small share of revenue, temporarily raise minSdk for the next release as a last resort; better is the real fix below, shipped as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) MultiDex.install missing, so classes2.dex is never loaded on Dalvik; (b) the main-dex list does not include AppGraph; (c) install-time dex extraction failing from low storage; (d) a ProGuard/R8 rule issue. (a) matches the symptom exactly: only the cohort on API < 21, and App.onCreate fails at the first class living in classes2.dex.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at the crash distribution by API level in Crashlytics; run apkanalyzer dex list app.apk / unzip -l to confirm there are classes2.dex; run the release variant on an API 19 emulator; check App for MultiDexApplication or attachBaseContext.
  5. Root cause: On Dalvik only classes.dex is loaded at start.
