Legacy multidex requires MultiDex.install(base) in attachBaseContext (or extending MultiDexApplication), which loads the secondary dex files before app code touches them. The bump pushed AppGraph into classes2.dex; before it, everything fit in one dex so the missing install went unnoticed.
  6. Fix: Short-term:
class App : Application() {
    override fun attachBaseContext(base: Context) {
        super.attachBaseContext(base)
        MultiDex.install(this)       // androidx.multidex:multidex:2.0.1
    }
}

or simply extends MultiDexApplication. Add androidx.multidex:multidex to dependencies. Long-term: reduce method count via R8, remove unused SDKs, and split features. 7. Prevention: Run CI release builds for the real minSdk (a minSdk19 device or emulator job runs the launch smoke test), add a build check on method count with alert at 90% of 65,536 per dex for legacy, and document the multidex requirement near minSdk. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not hand-curate a gigantic main-dex keep list to dodge install (slow, brittle). I would not drop API 19 silently before checking revenue, since product owns that call. Raising minSdk to 21 removes the legacy path entirely and is the cleanest long-term option.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same crash only on a few API 21+ devices? → Different cause: check ABI/class dedup, an OEM ROM that disabled native multidex, or a genuine missing class.
  • App is slower to start on 4.4 after the fix? → Yes: secondary dex extraction and optimisation on first launch (ANR risk on slow storage); mitigated by main-dex keep rules and not doing work before install.
  • What if the crash is in a ContentProvider rather than onCreate? → Providers run before Application.onCreate but after attachBaseContext, so install in attachBaseContext covers it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team added a crash-reporter initialised in a static block of a class in the secondary dex; the report was missing for the very crashes that mattered, because it also needed multidex to be installed first. They moved initialisation after MultiDex.install and tested legacy API on CI.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests random ProGuard changes; cannot connect the crash to Dalvik vs ART.
  • Hire: Identifies missing MultiDex.install/MultiDexApplication and the API < 21 correlation; applies fix and adds an old-API test.
  • Strong hire: Also explains main dex list, why CI missed it (flavour minSdk), startup-cost trade-offs, rollout halt, and the product decision on minSdk.

questions.contextHtml:
Your fitness app (minSdk 24, 4M DAU) ships a new "weekly summary" feature. The app code uses java.time only inside a third-party analytics SDK AAR (your code does not call it). Within hours: crash-free sessions drop from 99.6% to 96.8% on Android 7.x devices, which are 14% of users. Stack trace:

java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Ljava/time/LocalDate;
    at com.thirdparty.analytics.Scheduler.nextWindow(Scheduler.kt:88)
    at com.foo.stats.WeeklyJob.run(WeeklyJob.kt:23)

Lint was green. compileOptions sets sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17 and there is no isCoreLibraryDesugaringEnabled. The SDK's release notes say "supports API 21+ with library desugaring".
questions.promptHtml: Explain why only 7.x crashes, what D8 desugaring can and cannot do, and how you fix and prevent it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch" or "use ThreeTenABP" without understanding that Java 8 language features are desugared by default, but Java 8+ library APIs are not. They may also blame Kotlin or R8.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which OS versions crash (is it exactly API < 26)? Is the code mine or in a dependency? What AGP/desugar_jdk_libs versions? Is minSdk truly 24 in release? Was the SDK version bumped in this release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the SDK version or the feature behind a remote flag so the job never runs on API < 26; ship a hotfix with the proper fix next.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) java.time was introduced at API 26 and missing at runtime on 24/25; (b) a duplicate or older class shadows it; (c) R8 removed a class; (d) a bad Kotlin stdlib version. (a) fits "only 7.x" exactly.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics by API level; run the failing path on an API 25 emulator; apkanalyzer dex packages to look for j$.time (desugared) vs java.time references; check dependency's AAR with javap or look for the desugar_jdk_libs note in its docs.
  5. Root cause: D8 handles Java 8 language features (lambdas, default/static interface methods, try-with-resources) for any minSdk. It does not add newer library classes unless library (API) desugaring is on. With coreLibraryDesugaring, D8 rewrites references to java.time.* into a bundled j$.time.* copy. Lint did not flag it because the call is inside a dependency's bytecode, not source Lint analyses with NewApi.
  6. Fix: In the app module (AGP 4.0+):
android {
    compileOptions {
        sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
        targetCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
        isCoreLibraryDesugaringEnabled = true
    }
}
dependencies {
    coreLibraryDesugaring("com.android.tools:desugar_jdk_libs:2.0.4")   // use a current 2.x per AGP docs
}

Library desugaring applies to dependency bytecode too, so the SDK's java.time calls get rewritten. Long term: enable it in modules that expose APIs. 7. Prevention: Run a startup/smoke test on the minSdk emulator in CI; consider Lint on dependencies via lintChecks/checkDependencies; require third-party SDKs' minSdk and desugaring notes in the dependency review checklist. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Library desugaring adds some APK size and a few ms of DEX (the j$ classes), and not every JDK API is included (e.g., some java.util.concurrent and newer APIs differ). I would not raise minSdk to 26 just for this (lose 14% of users), and I would not use reflection hacks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does desugaring give me java.nio.file.Files or Stream on API 24? → Library desugaring covers many but not all; check the official supported list ("verify on developer.android.com").
  • Why did it only appear after this release? → The SDK's Scheduler code path was only reached by the new job.
  • Will it work with R8 disabled? → Desugaring is done by D8 regardless; R8 just also shrinks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that a "works on every device we own" release crashed only on API 25 tablets; no test device was below 26. They added an old-API emulator to the nightly pipeline and a dependency-review rule.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch or says "compileSdk 34 should include it".
  • Hire: Distinguishes language vs library desugaring and configures coreLibraryDesugaring.
  • Strong hire: Explains the D8 j$ rewrite, why Lint missed it, size trade-off, rollout mitigation and CI prevention.

questions.contextHtml: Your e-commerce app (8M installs, 70% Play, 30% sideloaded via enterprise MDM and OEM preload) has a cold start p50 of 1.1 s on a mid-range device on day 7, but p50 of 2.3 s and p95 of 4.8 s for users in their first launch after install. Day-1 retention is 8 points lower for the sideloaded group. After you enabled Baseline Profiles through the Gradle plugin last month, Play installs improved but sideloaded numbers did not. adb shell dumpsys package com.foo.app shows [status=verify] [reason=install] on a freshly installed sideloaded device. Product wants a plan within a week without raising the APK size.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and what you would change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do lazy init and remove SDKs" only. That is good practice but ignores that the same code runs 2x slower purely because it is unoptimised, and does not explain why Play and sideloaded differ.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the profile present inside the APK (assets/dexopt/baseline.prof, .dm)? Which AGP/Baseline Profile plugin version? Do sideloaded devices include androidx.profileinstaller? Which OS versions and how are the devices provisioned (MDM installs via PackageInstaller or adb)? Is background dexopt blocked by battery policy on those devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For managed devices, have MDM trigger a profile-based compile (cmd package compile -m speed-profile) post-install if the policy allows; otherwise accept the first-launch penalty while I fix the packaging.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) profile exists but is not applied on sideloaded installs (no Play-side .dm; no ProfileInstaller fallback); (b) the profile is stale (rules do not match R8-renamed methods because mapping changed); (c) heavy startup work unrelated to compile state; (d) storage or CPU throttling on cheap devices.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unzip the APK and look for assets/dexopt/baseline.prof and baseline.profm; adb shell dumpsys package dexopt for the state; dumpsys package ... | grep -A3 "Dexopt state" after adb shell cmd package compile -f -m speed-profile; Macrobenchmark CompilationMode.None() vs Partial() vs full to measure the upper bound.
  5. Root cause: On a plain sideload there is no Play cloud profile and no install-time profile compilation. The runtime has to interpret and JIT code until the idle/charging bg-dexopt job runs, which can take days on devices that rarely charge while idle. If ProfileInstaller is absent or its initializer disabled, the profile in the APK is never given to ART on that route.
  6. Fix: Short-term: add androidx.profileinstaller:profileinstaller (the library installs the profile on first launch, effective after the next app start), check the plugin generates the profile for the release variant, and refresh the profile each release. Long-term: add Startup Profiles for R8 DEX layout (colocating startup classes), cut startup work, track "first-launch" as its own metric.
// Macrobenchmark: compare compile states to prove the effect
@get:Rule val rule = MacrobenchmarkRule()
@Test fun startupNone() = rule.measureRepeated(
    packageName = "com.foo.app", metrics = listOf(StartupTimingMetric()),
    compilationMode = CompilationMode.None(), iterations = 10, startupMode = StartupMode.COLD
) { pressHome(); startActivityAndWait() }
  1. Prevention: Gate releases on a macrobenchmark with a profile, and monitor first-launch vs steady-state startup in field data (Android vitals, custom timer split by "install age").
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not force speed compilation of everything (install time, storage, larger dex2oat output) and I would not rely on users charging overnight. Profile installer takes effect only on the next start, so the very first launch is still slow; that is inherent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Profile applies but gains are small? → The bottleneck may be provider/SDK init, I/O or class verification, not compile mode; use a trace.
  • Does bundling the profile increase APK size? → A few hundred KB at most for typical profiles; verify in the APK Analyzer.
  • Does it help on Android 6? → No; profile-guided compilation needs Android 7+, and the full benefit with Play is Android 9+ in practice (verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped a 25% startup win in lab benchmarks with CompilationMode.Full, then saw no field gains, since real users ran the interpreter/JIT mix for the first days. They switched their benchmark to None/Partial to mirror real first-run, and fixed distribution.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only suggests removing SDKs or lazy init; does not mention compilation state.
  • Hire: Explains verify vs speed-profile, Play vs sideload difference, adds profileinstaller.
  • Strong hire: Verifies via dumpsys, uses Macrobenchmark with compilation modes, discusses Startup Profiles, metrics by install age and honest trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
After targeting API 34 and the new OS release rolling out, a "smart keyboard-aware chat" feature crashes for 2.4% of sessions (all on the latest OS version, which is 9% of your 3M DAU). Crashlytics:

java.lang.NoSuchFieldException: No field mShowing in class Landroid/widget/PopupWindow; (declaration of 'android.widget.PopupWindow' appears in /system/framework/framework.jar)
    at java.lang.Class.getDeclaredField(Native Method)
    at com.foo.ui.KeyboardHelper.<init>(KeyboardHelper.java:31)

The helper was copied from a Stack Overflow answer five years ago. QA tested on Android 12 and 13 only. Logcat on older versions shows Accessing hidden field Landroid/widget/PopupWindow;->mShowing:Z (unsupported, reflection, allowed).
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. How do you prevent repeats?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch and move on" without removing the dependency on an unsupported API, or "use a bypass library" which just defers the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which OS versions, devices? Are there other hidden API warnings in logs on the older versions? Is this our code or a library? What does the feature actually need (keyboard height, popup state)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag off the helper via remote config, or catch ReflectiveOperationException and fall back to a public-API path; ship it as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The field was moved from "unsupported/max-target" to blocked or renamed in the new OS; (b) obfuscation renamed it (no, it is framework code); (c) we are reading from a wrong class variant on some OEM builds; (d) device-specific. The logcat warnings on older versions strongly support (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run on the new OS emulator image; enable StrictMode.detectNonSdkApiUsage; scan the release APK and all dependencies with veridex to list every hidden API use, then look up the field in the AOSP hidden-API lists; check the AOSP source for that OS release (cs.android.com).
  5. Root cause: The app depended on a non-SDK internal field. Such interfaces can be restricted or removed with any release because they carry no compatibility promise. Tests on two old versions hid it.
  6. Fix: Short-term: tolerate failure.
class KeyboardHelper(private val popup: PopupWindow) {
    private val showingField: java.lang.reflect.Field? = try {
        PopupWindow::class.java.getDeclaredField("mShowing").apply { isAccessible = true }
    } catch (e: ReflectiveOperationException) { null }

    fun isShowing(): Boolean = showingField?.getBoolean(popup) ?: popup.isShowing
}

Better: delete the reflection and use public APIs, here PopupWindow.isShowing and WindowInsetsCompat/ime() insets (ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener) for keyboard state. 7. Prevention: Add veridex (or equivalent) to CI over the final APK; test on the newest preview/beta images through the Android beta program and am compat flags where relevant; add a Lint/detekt rule forbidding setAccessible on android.* classes; require a fallback when reflection is unavoidable. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not ship a hidden-API bypass library: version-specific, may violate Play policies on platform integrity, and breaks without notice. I would not rewrite the feature without checking the public insets API gives equivalent behaviour on API 21+.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The offending code is in a closed-source SDK? → Report to the vendor; pin the version, wrap or disable the feature, and prefer replacing the SDK; veridex shows which SDK.
  • Can R8 fix it? → No: R8 cannot grant access to framework-hidden members.
  • How do you know the new restrictions before users do? → Beta OS images, veridex on every release candidate, and watching the "non-SDK interface" notes in the behavior-changes pages.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team had three separate hidden-API users hidden in ad and image libraries; their veridex job caught two before the OS update, and a vendor ticket fixed the third in two weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds a try/catch or ignores the cause; no prevention.
  • Hire: Names hidden API restrictions as cause, uses detection tools, replaces with public API or fallback.
  • Strong hire: Establishes a prevention pipeline (veridex in CI, beta testing, lint rule), handles third-party SDK case and policy risk.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android verify an APK at install and update time? Explain signature schemes v1-v4, key rotation, and where Play App Signing fits.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Signing questions determine whether you can ship updates safely and understand tampering protection, a key point for release engineering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At install PackageManager verifies the APK's signature, checks it against any existing install of the same package (updates must be signed by the same certificate or a rotation lineage), and refuses on mismatch. Schemes evolved: v1 signs individual zip entries (JAR signing), v2 (Android 7.0) signs the whole APK file so tampering is detected quickly, v3 (Android 9) adds key rotation, v3.1 (Android 13) improves rotation targeting, and v4 (Android 11) is a separate Merkle-tree signature enabling incremental install. With Play App Signing, I sign my upload with an upload key and Play re-signs with the app signing key it holds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why identity matters: The signing certificate defines "who owns this package". Permissions with signature protection level, sharedUserId (deprecated) and updates all rely on it. Wrong key = INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE.
  • v1 (JAR): signature per file in META-INF/. Does not cover zip metadata; allows some tampering and is slow to verify.
  • v2 (API 24): signs the whole APK as a block between the zip entries and central directory; one hash verification. Apps targeting API 30+ must use v2 or newer.
  • v3 (API 28): includes a proof-of-rotation lineage so a new key can be trusted because the old key signed off on it. v3.1 (API 33): lets a rotated key apply from a specific SDK version upward; old OS versions continue to use the old key.
  • v4 (API 30): separate .idsig file with a Merkle tree, used for ADB incremental install (streaming) while v2/v3 still sign the APK.
  • Related: zipalign aligns uncompressed data (4-byte boundaries; native-lib page alignment is a separate topic) so ART can mmap; must be done before signing with v2+ (apksigner), because signing covers the aligned layout.
 build -> sign with upload key -> AAB to Play
 Play  -> split APKs -> sign with app signing key (Google-held)
 device-> PackageManager: verify v3/v2 -> compare with installed cert/lineage -> install

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
apksigner verify --verbose --print-certs app.apk      # shows v1..v4 status and certs
apksigner sign --ks release.jks --out signed.apk aligned.apk
zipalign -c -v 4 app.apk                               # verify alignment

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Losing the key (pre-Play App Signing) means no updates. Play App Signing mitigates by holding the app signing key.
  • Signing then zipaligning: this invalidates v2+ signatures; always zipalign first.
  • Mixing debug and release signatures on the same device: INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE; uninstall required, losing data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does sideloaded vs Play APK fail to update the other? → Different signing keys (upload key vs app signing key).
  2. Is rotation easy? → With v3/v3.1 and Play's flow, key rotation is possible but needs careful lineage; plan for older OS versions.
  3. What does Play Integrity or "signature verification" at runtime add? → Server-side attestation of app/device integrity; signature checks at runtime are tamper hints, not a security boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "APKs must be signed." Senior knows the scheme history, zipalign order, rotation lineage, Play upload vs app signing key, and diagnosing update failures.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team debugging "cannot update" for 400 enterprise users found an internal build signed with the upload key rather than the Play app signing key; the two never match by design.

questions.promptHtml: Beyond the basic Zygote fork, what are USAPs and app zygotes? What problem does each solve, and what are the trade-offs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes depth in process-start optimisation and security isolation. It separates people who know "Zygote forks" from those who know how the platform evolved.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The USAP pool (Android 10+) keeps a few pre-forked, unspecialised app processes ready, so a launch skips the fork and early setup and only pays for specialisation (uid, SELinux, ABI). The app zygote (Android 10+) is a per-app child zygote I can opt into for isolated services, preloading my own classes/data once so every isolated process forks from it. USAP trades idle memory for faster starts; app zygote trades complexity for faster, safer isolated processes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Problem with plain fork-on-demand: fork + specialisation happens on the critical path of a cold start, and it is serialised through Zygote's single select loop; many simultaneous launches queue behind each other.
  • USAP (unspecialized app process) pool: Zygote pre-forks N idle processes blocked on a socket. When system_server needs a process, it hands a pre-forked USAP its specialisation arguments and it continues immediately. Pool size is controlled by device config flags (tunable via DeviceConfig, with usap_pool_enabled style options, for OEMs/AOSP; I'd say "verify exact flag names" because they vary by release). Costs: always-resident small processes (memory), refill logic when the pool drains.
  • App zygote: declared by a service with android:isolatedProcess="true" and android:useAppZygote="true" (and optionally android:zygotePreloadName). The system forks a zygote for my app's uid range, runs my ZygotePreload class to load heavy shared state, and forks isolated processes from it. Isolated processes have no permissions and a separate uid; the preload gives them shared pages cheaply.
  • WebView zygote: a specific example; WebView renderers fork from it, sharing the preloaded Chromium code.
  • Security link: Zygote and its children use ASLR per-process (executables loaded at randomised bases, but pre-mapped regions are the same in the Zygote lineage, which is why relocation of shared libraries was a historical weakness; mitigations include per-fork re-randomisation of some regions). I would call this out as "design nuance, verify details in AOSP docs".
// AndroidManifest: an isolated service that forks from an app zygote
// <service android:name=".SandboxService"
//     android:isolatedProcess="true" android:useAppZygote="true"
//     android:zygotePreloadName=".MyPreload"/>
class MyPreload : android.app.ZygotePreload {
    override fun doPreload(appInfo: android.content.pm.ApplicationInfo) {
        // heavy, read-only shared state loaded once in the app zygote
        System.loadLibrary("sandbox_core")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking USAP is something apps configure; it is a platform/OEM setting.
  • Using app zygote for regular services; it only makes sense for isolated processes.
  • Preloading mutable or per-user state in the app zygote; it is shared across all isolated children.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does an isolated process help? → Parsing untrusted media/documents, plugin sandboxes.
  2. Does USAP change my Application.onCreate time? → No; it removes fork and early specialisation latency before my code starts.
  3. What is the memory cost? → A few idle processes' private RSS; typical designs keep the pool small.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows Zygote only. Senior can describe USAP motivation (contention on the fork path), app zygote's manifest contract, and where isolation makes sense.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A document-preview feature moved parsing into an isolatedProcess service with an app zygote preload for the native parser, cutting preview start by ~150 ms and removing a class of crashes from the main process.

questions.promptHtml: What is the system_server Watchdog, and what happens to my app when system_server hangs or crashes? How would I recognise this from an app developer's seat?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about failures below your app: when "the phone reboots itself" or every app stalls at once.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: system_server is one process hosting many services, so a deadlock in one lock can freeze others. The Watchdog thread periodically checks monitor locks and handler threads; if a check does not complete in about a minute, it dumps stacks and kills system_server. Because Zygote is tied to it, the Java framework restarts, a "soft reboot", and every app process dies. From the app side I see all my processes disappear, Process: system_server watchdog logs, or Binder calls into the system blocking.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Services such as AMS, ATMS, WMS and PMS are Java objects in one process, guarded by shared locks (for example the global AMS/WM lock). They execute on threads such as android.fg, android.ui, android.io, and a pool of Binder threads (the pool in system_server is larger than the typical app default of 15; commonly cited as 31; verify per release).
  • Watchdog: a thread that registers "monitors" (objects with monitor() that acquire locks) and handler threads. It posts checks; if a check does not return, it escalates: warn at half the timeout (30 s), kill at the full timeout (60 s in production, shorter in some debug configs; verify). On trigger it writes stack traces (to /data/anr / dropbox) and logs WATCHDOG KILLING SYSTEM PROCESS.
  • Consequences: system_server killed → Zygote notices, exits → init restarts Zygote and the whole main class → all apps restart (users see a boot animation without a full boot).
  • App-visible effects before the watchdog fires: blocked Binder calls from my main thread (e.g., startActivity, getPackageInfo, registerReceiver), producing jank or ANRs that are not my fault but still counted against my app. Apps cannot protect against it, only reduce synchronous system calls on the main thread.
  • Related: AMS also monitors app responsiveness (ANR) via input dispatch and broadcast/service timeouts; that logic runs inside system_server and is the other direction (system watching apps).
adb logcat -b all | grep -E "Watchdog|WATCHDOG|system_server"
adb bugreport                  # includes /data/anr and dropbox entries
adb shell dumpsys dropbox --print system_server_watchdog

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blaming the OEM or "random" reboot without reading dropbox / bugreport.
  • Believing apps can crash system_server; a normal app cannot, but a heavy Binder load (flooding a service) can contribute to lock contention.
  • Assuming your process "restarting by itself" is always an app bug; after a framework restart every app restarts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does a misbehaving app cause system_server contention? → Excessive synchronous Binder calls, large transactions, or storms of broadcasts/notifications/ContentObserver registrations.
  2. How do I tell app crash from framework restart? → In logcat, process start times for many unrelated pids reset; there's a kernel/Zygote restart marker and a different boot-id-like uptime for system_server.
  3. Can I observe this in production? → ApplicationExitInfo (API 30) gives a reason for my process death (e.g., REASON_OTHER, REASON_SIGNALED); correlate across a population.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "system_server is the core process." Senior can explain Watchdog mechanics, the soft reboot chain, how contention shows up as app ANRs, and how to use ApplicationExitInfo and bugreports to separate platform from app faults.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cluster of "app restarted for no reason" reports on one OEM build correlated with watchdog entries in bug reports; the cause was an OEM service deadlock, and the team stopped chasing a non-existent crash in their code.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app (5M DAU) upgrades AGP from 7.4 to 8.2 for a security requirement. The release candidate passes all instrumented tests (which run on the debug variant). In the 10% staged rollout, crash-free sessions drop from 99.7% to 97.1%. New top crashes:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodException: com.foo.model.Profile.<init> []
    at java.lang.Class.getConstructor0(Class.java:2332)
    at com.google.gson.internal.ConstructorConstructor...

and, on one screen, Gson-parsed objects have null for non-null Kotlin fields, then NPE. Retrofit calls with suspend functions fail with ClassCastException: Class cannot be cast to ParameterizedType. The proguard-rules.pro was written four years ago and has -keep class com.foo.model.** { *; } for only some packages. android.enableR8.fullMode is not set in gradle.properties.
questions.promptHtml: What changed, how do you stabilise the rollout, and how do you prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable minify" permanently (APK grows, no obfuscation) or randomly adding -keep class ** { *; }. They do not know AGP 8 made R8 full mode the default, so old rules no longer protect reflective use.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which libraries use reflection (Gson, Retrofit, Moshi reflective, Firebase)? Is the crash on all OS versions? Do we upload mapping files? What changed except AGP? Did the release variant ever run instrumented tests?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout and release a hotfix with android.enableR8.fullMode=false in gradle.properties to restore compat mode (as a stopgap; the option may be removed in future AGPs), or roll back to the previous AGP build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) full mode no longer keeps default constructors of classes referenced via reflection unless a rule says so; (b) generic signature/annotation attributes stripped, breaking Gson TypeToken and Retrofit suspend return types; (c) fields renamed for model classes outside the kept packages; (d) library consumer rules changed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build the release variant locally and inspect mapping.txt, usage.txt (-printusage), seeds.txt; run Crashlytics de-obfuscated traces; use -whyareyoukeeping for key classes; run a smoke/instrumented suite against release with testBuildType = "release"; diff output with apkanalyzer.
  5. Root cause: R8 full mode is more aggressive: it no longer implicitly keeps default constructors, may merge classes/inline more, and drops generic Signature and annotations not explicitly kept. Rules that worked in compat mode implied behaviours full mode no longer provides. The tests ran the unminified debug build, so nothing exercised the shrunk code.
  6. Fix: Short-term as above. Proper rules:
# Keep what reflection needs
-keepattributes Signature, *Annotation*, InnerClasses, EnclosingMethod
-keep class com.foo.model.** { <init>(...); <fields>; }
-keepclassmembers,allowobfuscation class * { @com.google.gson.annotations.SerializedName <fields>; }
# Retrofit/Gson versions ship consumer rules; upgrade them (suspend + full mode support varies by version)

Long term: replace reflection-based parsing with codegen (kotlinx.serialization, Moshi codegen / KSP), which needs few keep rules and is safe under shrinking. 7. Prevention: Run tests/smoke on the release (minified) variant in CI, upload mapping to Crashlytics, review usage.txt in PRs touching rules, add a rule-free-model policy (annotated models), and stage rollouts at 1-5% with automated halt on crash-rate. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not keep everything (-keep class ** { *; }): bigger APK, no optimisation, hides future issues. I would not leave compat mode on indefinitely; it is deprecated and loses optimisations. Full mode's smaller/faster code is worth the one-time rule cleanup.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It only fails on Android 7? → Likely a different issue (e.g. desugaring or JIT difference); check by API and R8 library versions.
  • Is turning off obfuscation OK? → It is not a fix; shrinking without obfuscation (-dontobfuscate) still removes members. Obfuscation and shrinking are separate switches.
  • How do you find which rule keeps what? → seeds.txt, -whyareyoukeeping class X, and -printconfiguration.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team had rules referencing packages that had been moved two years earlier; nothing matched, and it only worked because compat mode kept more. The AGP upgrade exposed the debt; moving models to codegen retired the rule file's risk entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Disables minify or adds blanket keeps; no staged rollout logic.
  • Hire: Identifies R8 full mode and missing attributes/constructors; uses the compat flag as stopgap and fixes rules.
  • Strong hire: Explains the shrinking mechanics, tests release variants, moves to codegen, and sets rollout guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
A new "document scanner" feature loads a native library from a vendor AAR. QA's emulator and several devices pass. In production, crash rate for the feature is 0% on most devices but 100% for the feature on about 1.4% of daily users (about 70k sessions), all on devices reported as arm64 (new mid-range phones). Crash:

java.lang.UnsatisfiedLinkError: dlopen failed: library "libscannercore.so" not found
    at java.lang.Runtime.loadLibrary0(Runtime.java:1087)
    at com.vendor.scanner.Native.<clinit>(Native.java:12)

The APK contents:

lib/arm64-v8a/libfoo_image.so         (our own library)
lib/armeabi-v7a/libfoo_image.so
lib/armeabi-v7a/libscannercore.so      (vendor)

ndk { abiFilters += listOf("arm64-v8a", "armeabi-v7a") } is set. The vendor says "armeabi-v7a runs on arm64 devices."
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, how Android picks a native ABI, and how to fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the missing library" or "ask the vendor to fix" without understanding why the lib is not found even though a compatible 32-bit version exists in the APK.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which devices fail (arm64 only?), are they 64-bit-only (many newer phones)? Does the vendor ship arm64-v8a? Is libscannercore.so in the 64-bit directory? Is anyone using android:extractNativeLibs? Is the loaded lib from our own code or the vendor's System.loadLibrary?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the feature through a remote flag for arm64 devices if the vendor has no 64-bit lib; if the vendor is unreachable, as a stopgap, ship armeabi-v7a only (removing arm64 libs so the process runs 32-bit) but note that this breaks on 64-bit-only devices and Play requirements, so it is a short-term trade.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the vendor lacks an arm64-v8a build, and the system chose arm64-v8a because we shipped an arm64 lib; (b) the lib is not extracted/packaged due to ABI filter; (c) the lib depends on another missing .so; (d) device/ROM-specific. (a) fits: only arm64 devices, mixed ABIs.
  4. How I'd verify each: unzip -l app.apk | grep lib/; apkanalyzer files list; on device adb shell pm dump com.foo.app | grep -i abi (primaryCpuAbi); readelf -h / file on .so files; check Build.SUPPORTED_ABIS logs.
  5. Root cause: The system selects one ABI per app process (primary ABI), based on the native libraries present in the APK and the device's supported ABIs in preference order. Since we shipped arm64-v8a libs, the process is started as 64-bit and only lib/arm64-v8a/ is searched. The vendor lib exists only in armeabi-v7a, which a 64-bit process cannot load (no mixing of 32- and 64-bit code in one process). So libscannercore.so is "not found".
  6. Fix: Get a 64-bit build from the vendor, or replace the SDK. For the packaging, make ABI sets consistent across all native deps; verify in CI. Example check:
android {
    defaultConfig { ndk { abiFilters += listOf("arm64-v8a", "armeabi-v7a") } }
    // CI: assert every .so name present in one ABI directory exists in all the others
}

And guard at runtime:

fun scannerAvailable(): Boolean = try {
    System.loadLibrary("scannercore"); true
} catch (e: UnsatisfiedLinkError) { false }
  1. Prevention: A Gradle task or script comparing .so sets across ABIs on every build, a device-farm test on a 64-bit-only device, vendor SDK checklist requires arm64-v8a.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not drop the arm64 libraries to force 32-bit mode permanently: Play requires 64-bit support for apps with native code, and 64-bit-only devices exist. I would not rely on 32-bit emulation or translation layers (e.g. x86 emulators translating ARM) as a design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Works on QA's x86 emulator? → Translation layers can run ARM libs on x86; production arm64 behaviour is stricter. Test on real ARM devices.
  • extractNativeLibs=false? → Libs are loaded straight from the APK (must be page-aligned/stored uncompressed); doesn't change ABI selection.
  • What does Play deliver via AAB? → The ABI split for the device; a missing lib for that ABI is still missing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped a camera SDK with 32-bit-only vendor code for two years; the first 64-bit-only flagship launch turned a 0.1% crash into a loud one. They added the ABI-parity check to CI.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says "armeabi-v7a should work on arm64" or blames the vendor only.
  • Hire: Explains one ABI per process, 32/64 mixing is impossible, fixes packaging or gets 64-bit lib.
  • Strong hire: Adds CI parity check, runtime guard and flag, discusses Play 64-bit requirement and emulation pitfalls.

questions.contextHtml:
Your app embeds a plugin system for partner "mini-tools". It downloads a .jar (with dex) over HTTPS, saves it to filesDir/plugins/ and loads it with DexClassLoader. You bump targetSdk from 33 to 34. QA on Android 14 reports the plugin screen opens and immediately crashes. In staged rollout, 2.2% of sessions crash on Android 14 devices (30% of fleet) while Android 13 is fine.

java.lang.SecurityException: Writable dex file '/data/user/0/com.foo.app/files/plugins/tool_v3.jar' is not allowed.
    at dalvik.system.DexFile.openDexFileNative(Native Method)
    at dalvik.system.DexClassLoader.<init>(DexClassLoader.java:59)
val f = File(filesDir, "plugins/tool_v3.jar")
download(url, f)
val cl = DexClassLoader(f.absolutePath, codeCacheDir.absolutePath, null, classLoader)
questions.promptHtml: What changed, how do you fix it, and what else should you worry about with dynamic code loading?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert targetSdk to 33" as the only plan, or "chmod the file" using shell tricks. They do not know the behaviour is tied to targetSdk 34 or its security rationale.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash appear only on API 34 with targetSdk 34 (confirm with a build of targetSdk 33 on the same device)? Where do plugin files come from? Are they integrity-checked? Does anything modify the file after download? Is this feature required for 100% of users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause rollout of the targetSdk bump; or hotfix with the read-only change (fast) behind the same release; plugin screen can be hidden by a flag for API 34+ until the hotfix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Android 14 requires dynamically loaded dex/jar/apk files to be read-only for apps targeting API 34; (b) a file permission problem from storage; (c) a corrupted download; (d) a missing codeCacheDir. The message "Writable dex file ... is not allowed" is explicit.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce on an Android 14 emulator with targetSdk 34, then flip the compat change off via adb shell am compat disable <CHANGE_NAME> com.foo.app if the change ID is known from the behaviour-changes page; log file.canWrite(); read the Android 14 "safer dynamic code loading" doc.
  5. Root cause: Android 14 hardens code injection: for apps targeting API 34, files loaded via DexClassLoader (and similar) must not be writable by the app, because a writable code file is an attack surface (any bug that writes to app storage becomes code execution). Our code writes then loads without removing write permission.
  6. Fix: Mark the file read-only before loading; load via a freshly written file to avoid writing again; verify integrity.
val f = File(filesDir, "plugins/tool_v3.jar")
download(url, f)
verifySha256(f, expectedHash)              // integrity before execution
f.setReadOnly()                            // required for targetSdk 34+ before loading
val cl = DexClassLoader(f.absolutePath, codeCacheDir.absolutePath, null, classLoader)

If an update is needed, write a new versioned file (or delete the read-only file then recreate), instead of overwriting in place. Long-term: prefer Play Feature Delivery (dynamic feature modules) for first-party features, which is the supported mechanism and passes Play policy. 7. Prevention: Add targetSdk bump to a checklist with behaviour-change review; test with the new target on a real Android 14 device before staged rollout; write an integration test for plugin load. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not keep targetSdk at 33 indefinitely (Play requires up-to-date targeting). I would not skip signature/hash checks: downloading and executing code is high-risk and Google Play policy restricts downloading executable code outside Play for apps distributed there; confirm the plugin design complies (I'd say "verify current Play policy").

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does this apply to native libraries loaded from filesDir? → The docs cover dex and JAR primarily; native code loading is also restricted by other rules (e.g. SELinux, no exec from app data on newer targets) so I'd verify per release.
  • Why not just keep setReadOnly at download time? → That's fine; the requirement is read-only at load time.
  • Does a read-only file get hijacked by other apps? → App-private filesDir is not accessible to other apps; the danger is the app itself or a root/injection scenario.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's plugin loader had a write-then-load race with a background updater; the read-only change surfaced the bug that two threads re-wrote the same file. They moved to versioned filenames and atomic rename.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reverts targetSdk, or tries shell/chmod hacks.
  • Hire: Names the Android 14 read-only requirement, applies setReadOnly(), verifies it on API 34.
  • Strong hire: Adds integrity checks, versioned files, Play policy awareness, and a targetSdk-bump playbook.

questions.subtopic: Build pipeline from source to installed code
questions.promptHtml: Describe what happens to my Kotlin code from ./gradlew assembleRelease to code running on a device. Which tools touch it, and which of them can break a release build that works in debug?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the toolchain well enough to debug release-only failures and size/perf trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Kotlin compiler produces .class files, then AGP merges them with library classes. R8 (the default shrinker/optimiser) shrinks, obfuscates and optimises, and its built-in D8 stage desugars and converts to DEX. AAPT2 compiles and links resources and the manifest; the pieces are packaged, zipaligned and signed into an APK or AAB. Release-only breakage typically comes from R8 (reflection, missing keep rules), resource shrinking, manifest merge differences, and signing config.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
.kt/.java --kotlinc/javac--> .class ┐
libs (AAR/JAR, consumer rules) ─────┤
                                    v
                      R8: shrink -> optimise -> obfuscate -> desugar -> DEX
                                    |
res/ + manifests --AAPT2 compile/link--> resources.arsc + merged manifest
                                    v
        package (APK/AAB) -> (resource shrink) -> zipalign -> sign (apksigner)
  • Debug vs release differ in: minification (isMinifyEnabled), isShrinkResources, debuggable, signing config, BuildConfig.DEBUG, and often network/security config. Debug uses D8 only (no shrinking), so reflection "just works".
  • R8 steps: tree shaking (unused code removed), optimisation (inlining, class merging, devirtualisation, with full mode more aggressive), obfuscation (renaming; mapping file generated), desugaring (Java 8+ language features, optional library desugaring), DEX output; also generates a main-dex list for legacy multidex.
  • Resource shrinking removes unused resources based on R8's code reachability; dynamic string-based lookups (getIdentifier) may need keep.xml.
  • Manifest merge: library manifests merge into the app's; conflicts resolved with tools:node/tools:replace; exported flags and permissions often differ from the expectation, only seen in the merged manifest (app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/).
  • Output differences: APK for direct install, AAB for Play; split generation happens in bundletool/Play, not Gradle.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true
            isShrinkResources = true
            proguardFiles(getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"), "proguard-rules.pro")
        }
    }
}
./gradlew :app:assembleRelease -Pandroid.enableR8.fullMode=true   # (default in AGP 8+)
apkanalyzer dex packages --defined-only app-release.apk

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only running debug builds in CI and shipping untested release code.
  • Forgetting to archive mapping.txt per release; stack traces become unreadable.
  • Resource shrinking silently removing resources referenced by string.
  • Assuming R8 and ProGuard are identical; R8 reads ProGuard rule syntax but behaves differently.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Kotlin metadata fit with R8? → Kotlin reflection/serialization may need the kotlin.Metadata kept; R8 has Kotlin-aware handling, but libraries using kotlin-reflect need rules.
  2. How do I debug an R8 issue? → Inspect mapping.txt, usage.txt, seeds.txt; use -whyareyoukeeping; compare debug vs release on a device.
  3. Why is AAB not a build target for installs? → An AAB is a publishing format; devices install APK splits generated by Play or bundletool.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "R8 shrinks and obfuscates." Senior walks the whole chain, ties each stage to specific release-only failure modes and the artifacts to inspect (merged manifest, mapping, usage), and builds CI to cover them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's release-only crash came from the merged manifest: a library added android:exported="true" on an activity, which the debug flavour had overridden with tools:node="merge" only in debug sources. Reading the final merged manifest of the release variant found it in minutes.
